blocks.x: Shopify introduced Canvas, a site-building tool that lets merchants set up their store by chatting with AI. Its earlier no-code builder meant rearranging a theme's sections and blocks, and deeper customization required code or a developer.

In Canvas, merchants chat with Shopify's AI agent, Sidekick, and see changes in real time. It isn't a static preview but the store's real code being rendered, so merchants can test interactivity and animation across screen sizes; Sidekick also takes screenshots to see what the merchant sees.
Merchants can still click elements to edit directly. Shopify gave Sidekick the ability to work directly with theme files and simplified the theme architecture so it can understand and change it.

Third-party themes, app blocks and extensions, markets, translations, rollouts and theme updates aren't in the initial launch, and Canvas is desktop-only; Shopify says it plans to support these over time.

Nine in 10 developers use at least one AI tool at work, per a JetBrains survey, but AI coding tools learned from a largely inaccessible web. WebAIM's latest report found average issues per page rose 10% year over year, naming AI-assisted code a likely contributor.

AudioEye gave five AI tools (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, xAI and Lovable) the same brief: build three websites meeting WCAG at the AA standard. All 15 sites failed WCAG Level A, averaging 55 issues per page, close to the typical site's 62. 91% of issues were medium or high severity.
Yet 81% of teams using AI tools are confident their AI-generated code meets accessibility guidelines, while 50% of that group have noticed more issues and complaints since adopting AI.
46% of surveyed organizations using AI received an accessibility complaint, demand letter or lawsuit in the last 24 months. The piece is written by AudioEye CEO Kelly Georgevich.

Brand designers use many of the same building blocks as product designers, such as type, color and layout. In this Workflow Lab, a designer at the fictional Museum of Speculative Futures (MOSF) brings the design system from Figma Design into Figma Weave to build an exhibition campaign: a poster, a billboard and social posts.

blocks.cap: Elements from the brand designer and the MOSF design system used as input in Weave

blocks.x: Layout and swatch frames are pasted onto the Weave canvas as Figma nodes and connected to an Image Describer. Photos of the exhibition installations run through the same setup, and the Gen Effect node pushes the imagery further, returning something slightly different each run.
The Figma node sends each image back into Figma Design frames with editable text, and social posts are localized for French, German, Japanese and Portuguese markets.

blocks.cap: The exhibition poster

blocks.x: Because the Figma nodes stay connected, a new color token or type style updates the frame in Figma, the node in Weave, and reruns the baseline.

Chat will always be just an interface. Agents are not, and the design work has moved to the contract underneath your product. DataDome counted 17.7 billion AI agent requests in Q2 2026, up 45% from the quarter before.

In headless AI, the UI becomes a client rather than the product. The author suggests sorting 30 days of requests and sequencing agent calls into journeys: a retry loop is confusion, a call that always precedes an abandon is a dead end.

Map every door into the product, including APIs, webhooks and MCP servers; constraints that lived only in the interface were never really constraints. The craft is service design plus API literacy: field names, scopes and the tool description a model reads.
Error strings become the only recovery interface an agent sees, so design for partial success, idempotent writes and explicit confirmation, and measure task completion rather than page views.

blocks.cap: Before and after AI Light 2.0. Noise drops in scenes with many light sources.

blocks.x: Otoy has begun releasing a public alpha of OctaneRender 2027.1, the next major version of its GPU renderer. It is an experimental build separate from the stable OctaneRender 2026.

The biggest change is a real-time 'neural rendering' mode. It builds on the Neural Radiance Cache (NRC) added in OctaneRender 2026, combining Nvidia DLSS Ray Reconstruction with Otoy's own research. Otoy says this allows "near noise-free interactive rendering" with far fewer samples than traditional path tracing, even in complex lighting. For now it is Windows and Linux only; Octane X for Mac will get it later.
On upscaling, DLSS 4 and AMD FSR 3 have been added. Because OctaneRender is CUDA-based, FSR 3 also only runs on Nvidia GPUs.

AI Light, which samples multiple light sources, has had its first major change since debuting in OctaneRender 4.0. It now factors in both spatial and directional information for each emissive primitive, so there is less noise at the same sample count.
USD now supports geometry export as well as import. The standalone version gets a USD stage editor, and MaterialX adds three new EDF nodes. The per-primitive UV map limit has also risen from 3 to 10.

blocks.cap: Iridescent surfaces made with Alpha 2's Physical Optics material

blocks.x: Alpha 2 added a Physical Optics material that reproduces wave-optics effects such as diffraction, thin-film interference, and birefringence, covering everything from soap bubbles to brushed metal, holographic stickers, and CD surfaces. A retroreflective material that sends light straight back toward its source was also added — think traffic signs or reflective safety vests.

blocks.cap: SDF mesh baking added in Alpha 3

blocks.x: Alpha 3 adds the ability to bake SDFs, including Vectron primitives, into polygon meshes, for creating proxy geometry used in scattering or physics simulation. It also supports OCIO 2.5.

Before the stable release, Otoy plans to add more features, including anime/sketch renderers, 3D Gaussian splat rendering, AI functions such as built-in PBR material generation, and Otoy Studio integration. Since the first alpha arrived in March 2026, the stable release is likely around year-end. An Octane Studio+ subscription costs €23.95 a month or €239.88 a year.

Which MCP server should you connect so a coding agent can draw app screens, icons, or illustrations as SVG? This piece, first published by SVG Lab, puts its own SVG Lab MCP at the top of the list — worth keeping in mind while reading.

The author sees picking the wrong type of server as the most common mistake. Design MCP servers fall into three categories: design engines that return a fully laid-out result from a single request; editor connectors — like Figma, Penpot, and SVGator — where the model directly manipulates documents in an app you already use; and generators (SVGMaker, SVG Genie, SVG AI, CleanVector) that spit out one SVG file per prompt.

The difference matters to an agent. A generator hands over only a file, leaving the rest of the setup to the agent. An editor connector requires having that editor on hand, usually with a paid seat. A design engine saves the finished result in its own project space.

SVG Lab MCP turns mobile and web screens, components, icon sets, illustrations, and charts into SVG. The engine handles spacing, alignment, and text fitting, while the model only fills in content. It can't animate or vectorize images, and requires a Plus ($20/month, 5,000 generations) or Max ($40/month, 15,000 generations) plan.

Figma's remote server originally only read design context for code generation. Now it writes frames, components, variables, and auto layout directly into files. Canvas writes are free during the beta and will later switch to usage-based pricing, requiring a Full seat. The open-source Penpot reads and edits a file's components, styles, and tokens, but needs a Penpot tab open. SVGator is built for motion, not screen layout.

Among the generators, SVGMaker is open source under the MIT license, and SVG Genie only charges for successful generations. Using MCP with SVG AI requires a paid account, and CleanVector has folded MCP into its Plus and Pro plans. Outside this list, Canva also runs an MCP server — connecting is free, with only some features requiring a paid plan.

blocks.cap: Adobe MAX venue (Image: Adobe)

blocks.x: Creative Bloq's Tom May recalls a moment from the 2023 MAX keynote. Adobe Digital Media president David Wadhwani boasted that more than 3 billion images had been generated since Firefly's launch, but the crowd responded with silence rather than cheers. It was a moment that revealed how working creatives really feel about generative AI.

This year's MAX runs November 10–12 in Miami Beach. What will be announced isn't known yet, but the list of 208 sessions has been published, and May read through all of them to work out Adobe's current priorities.

Adobe is still putting its full weight behind generative AI. What's changed is that it now knows people may dislike it. The AI track, made up of 25 sessions, repeats lines like "we're not trying to replace craft" and "a creative partner, not a crutch." There's even a session titled 'AI Is Not Our Titanic.'

Scroll further down the AI sessions and the main audience isn't individual designers or freelancers. It's marketing leads, agency heads, and procurement staff buying software in bulk. Firefly Graph pitches "governance, scalability, and indemnification," and Omnicom is showing off an "agentic operating model." One agency boasts of producing over a million assets for brands like eBay, Spotify, and Just Eat.

blocks.cap: An Adobe stage under the banner 'The Future of Creativity in the Age of AI' (Image: Adobe)

blocks.x: The sharpest contrast is Toni Harmer's all-day Illustrator workshop, billed as learning traditional skills 'without AI.' Going without AI is now the exception. Plenty of sessions still cater to working pros, of course — Aaron Draplin's logo talk, David Blatner's InDesign tips, and a deep dive into Lightroom masking among them.

What May thinks designers actually want isn't AI that does the work for them. It's AI that takes care of grunt work — removing noise in Premiere, masking skies in Lightroom — plus honesty about pricing and training data. But the overall direction leans toward scale, volume, and enterprise buyers. One session asks, "If everyone can make things, what matters is who does?" May writes that Adobe's current answer looks like 'whoever buys the enterprise license.'

blocks.cap: Meta Muse Charm

blocks.x: Public opinion on AI is souring, with growing worries about mass unemployment and even human extinction. Meta is dialing down the scariness and turning up the cuteness in its new AI agent Muse and its dedicated device. It's betting on 'kawaii' as its pitch for selling AI hardware to the public.

Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg unveiled the handheld device Muse Charm at Meta Connect on Wednesday. It looks like a futuristic Tamagotchi, and the chatbot on its screen appears as a round, beige, furry mascot. Users choose its name; Instagram's Adam Mosseri named his 'Max.'
Zuckerberg said, "We've packed the entire Muse experience — down to real-time voice and the avatar stack — into a device the size of a keychain, so you can talk to it anytime."

It's not a glowing orb like Siri, nor a cursor and text like ChatGPT. Meta chose a cute monster avatar instead — a sign that big tech companies are appealing to soft emotion in the race to go mainstream.

Muse reads emails, books classes, drafts documents, and even shops. It's blocked on Amazon. Handing over multiple account permissions requires trust, which has long been a weak spot for Meta and other social media companies. Still, if Muse succeeds, it could prove that a mascot eases AI anxiety better than a disembodied voice or orb.

Cuteness shows up in transportation, too. Zoox's robotaxi, Amazon's delivery vans, and DoorDash's delivery robot Dot are all designed to look round and unthreatening. Research suggests cuteness triggers a desire to nurture — the opposite feeling from the fear many Americans hold toward AI.

Zuckerberg pitched Muse Charm as a device you use without unlocking your phone or opening an app. The materials and components are still being finalized and pricing isn't set, but Meta plans to launch it in time for the year-end holiday season. How much demand there will be remains unknown.

This week Meta also unveiled its next-generation smart glasses without a camera, part of a push to offer a device free of covert-recording controversy. With a cute mascot living inside a rounded rectangular gadget, Meta is trying to dull the edge of a technology consumers fear.

blocks.cap: Simulink Copilot chat screen

blocks.x: MathWorks has announced MATLAB and Simulink release 2026b (R2026b). New products include Simulink Variant Manager, Visual Inspection Toolbox, and Polyspace Test Server, alongside expanded capabilities for aerospace, embedded systems, AI, cognition, audio, and statistical analysis.

The backdrop is complexity. As software, electronics, and AI become intertwined in a single system, the number of design variants teams must manage and verify has grown. R2026b targets that burden with configuration management, vision inspection, automated testing, and system verification tools.

Visual Inspection Toolbox combines AI with image processing techniques to let users develop and deploy vision inspection applications for manufacturing and industrial sites. Point Cloud Toolbox gained workflows for lidar, cameras, radar, and SLAM.

Simulink Variant Manager is a tool for managing product variants across models and system architectures, keeping consistency and traceability in product-line or platform-based design. Polyspace Test Server automatically runs testing and code coverage analysis for C/C++ embedded software in CI environments.

Simulink now includes AI-based profiling insights from Simulink Copilot. It also gained published models that can be reused without rebuilding, and a JSON data dictionary for source control. Deep Learning Toolbox added a Time Series Modeler app for time-series AI, and PyTorch models can now run alongside MATLAB and Simulink.

Hardware-software co-design falls to SoC Blockset for AMD, which gained more capabilities for AMD adaptive SoCs and FPGAs. MATLAB itself picked up TOML-based project files, File Exchange package management, and Google Sheets integration.
Google has shown a new way to use its AI UI design tool Stitch. The core idea is to put real brand assets at the center of AI design.

In a September 24 post, Stitch's official account demonstrated dragging a brand kit and product images into the prompt box. The model is Gemini 3.8 Flash. Stitch pulls design-system information and style from the brand assets, then builds layouts for marketing and product pages. Product photos aren't treated as files dropped into a fixed template, but as material woven naturally into the layout.

This isn't an entirely new feature launch. Stitch has accepted image input since it first launched in 2025, and a 2026 update added URL-based design-system extraction and DESIGN.md, which exchanges reusable design rules. Gemini 3.8 Flash also became Stitch's default model in early September.

What stands out is that the AI-made screens aren't just convincing on their own -- they help stay consistent with the existing brand. Instead of phrases like 'premium and modern,' you hand over the visuals that actually define the brand, which is especially useful for e-commerce teams or designers building campaign pages.

The reaction hasn't been all positive. Some asked whether it also understands a brand's 'forbidden rules,' like spots where a logo must never go, and some users called the results 'AI slop.' Google hasn't yet disclosed which design tokens and rules it extracts, supported file formats and upload limits, how broad the coverage is, or how much human cleanup is needed.
The real test lies beyond the polished demo. Whether Stitch can honor even small brand rules and cut down on human touch-up remains to be seen.
Adobe announced it is bringing its software and tools directly into Google's AI platform Gemini. This follows similar moves with ChatGPT, Claude, Slack and Copilot.

Gemini is an AI assistant with over a billion monthly users. The new 'Adobe in Gemini' lets people direct Gemini to use professional-grade tools from Photoshop, Lightroom, Express and Firefly for a range of tasks. The entire process happens through conversation with Gemini.

Neal Pancholi, who leads GDM and Gemini global partnerships at Google, said: "We're excited to expand our partnership with Adobe to bring industry-leading creative tools directly into Gemini. Now anyone can create, edit, and bring ideas to life right within chat."

Adobe gave this example: upload several photos at once, and Gemini uses Adobe's correction tools to unify their tone and color. It refines lighting and color, crops to the size you want, and prepares the result for immediate use. It can also create social-media versions that keep a company's own branding and mood, or build custom Express templates on the fly.

Adobe called this launch a 'first step' in its relationship with Google. Adobe, which is already embedding agentic AI inside its own apps, appears intent on using AI to help people reach the result they want quickly without opening an app.

Adobe explained: "AI chatbot platforms have made it easier than ever to turn an idea into a tangible output. But reaching the result you actually want takes more than that," adding, "Images need refining, designs need customizing, and content needs adjusting for each channel. That's where the depth of our tools shows."
Adobe in Gemini has begun rolling out and is available on every Gemini plan, though it requires an Adobe account.

An AI photo editor's screen looks simple: upload, prompt, settings, generate -- done. But the implementation is far trickier, because every single control is tied to a 'capability contract' that keeps changing. The author says they wrote a draft with AI's help, then revised it against ArtDo's actual workflow.

The question to ask isn't 'how do I add one more model to the dropdown.' It's how to keep the UI from ever offering a request the chosen workflow can't handle, and how to make sure the result can be reviewed later.

So the request is treated as a state, not a loose input form. Without explicitly defining stages -- no source selected, validating, loading capability info, selecting compatible settings, preparing the request, generating, awaiting review, revise/download -- a combination the current model doesn't support can slip through while a user picks a resolution and then switches modes. The submit button only lights up when source, model, settings, account status, and the latest capability data all line up.

Values like the model list, image count, aspect ratio, resolution, and credit cost change often. Baking them into copy creates two sources of truth. The copy should only explain the workflow and its limits, the actual choices should be drawn from live capability data, and the final request should be checked once more on the server.

When switching models invalidates other settings, valid values should be kept and invalid ones reset to a supported default. Quietly leaving an invalid value in place is the most dangerous option. While capability info is reloading, submission should be blocked, and a previous model's options should never be shown as if they belonged to the current one.

The prompt is also part of validation. Writing down what should change, what should stay, and what tends to drift makes it easier to judge whether the result met the conditions. Generation-complete and review-complete are treated as separate states too. The original and the result, the prompt, and the settings should be compared side by side, and only after a human checks vulnerable spots -- faces, small text, hands, reflections -- should it move on to download.

Failure is part of the product too. Validation, provider, safety, account, and network errors shouldn't be flattened into one message -- users need to know whether to fix the input, log in, or retry. In the end, the contract you can actually defend is far narrower than 'edit anything perfectly.' It means showing only compatible choices, honestly marking generation and failure, and handing back a result for a human to review.

If you've ever opened Blender, been overwhelmed by its complex interface, and closed it within minutes, so has the author. After watching Flow -- made entirely in Blender and winner of the 2025 Academy Award for Best Animated Feature -- they wanted to try it, but kept giving up in the face of panels, menus, and hundreds of settings.

That wall is coming down. Earlier this year, Blender released an official MCP (Model Context Protocol) server, which connects AI models like Claude or ChatGPT to Blender so they can work directly inside the app. Describe the scene you want in words, and the chatbot builds it -- or at least most of it. Using this approach, the author, who had never used Blender before, made a 45-second animation in about three to four hours.

They used Claude Opus 5.5 in low effort mode, which cost about 26% of a session's usage on the $20 Pro plan. Of the four hours, less than one hour was spent hands-on; most of it went to reviewing results and re-describing what they wanted, while Claude worked alone for stretches of several hours the rest of the time. The published video is the third version -- camera movement, the character model, and background depth all had issues that took several rounds to fix.

blocks.cap: A wide view of the world Claude built in Blender

blocks.x: They also learned a working order. At first they asked Claude to start in a small area and zoom out to reveal the whole scene, but detail thinned out the farther it pulled back. So instead they had it build out the entire world in as much detail as possible first, then focus on one point and pull out from there -- similar to mapping out a world and its setting before handling characters in a story.

Setup takes about 10 minutes. Claude's 'computer use' feature can also control Blender, but that requires handing over the whole computer and burns a lot of tokens on constant screenshots. With the MCP server, Claude and Blender can run separately while you do other things. Install the MCP add-on on Blender 5.1 or later, turn on online access in preferences, and start the server. On Claude's side, just download the .mcpb file and install it as an extension. The Blender window needs to stay open, not minimized.

blocks.cap: Flaws remained too, like the robot's head clipping through flower petals

blocks.x: The video isn't perfect. The robot floats off the ground for no reason, and its head sinks into a flower when it touches one. Still, the author finds meaning in the fact that someone who'd always been intimidated by Blender sat with the interface for four hours and learned it. AI slop is a problem of shipping low-quality output straight to consumers, they say; using AI to learn a new tool is a different story.

At Frontify's Paradigms conference on the Croatian island of Obonjan, the most interesting talk came not from a design studio but from the creative director of a federal agency. NASA creative director David Rager spoke about managing NASA's visual brand and graphic standards manual, and about the 'worm' logo, revived in 2020.

His career hasn't followed a straight path. He got into graphic design while playing in a band, making flyers and album covers, and went on to work at museums, agencies, a Paris architecture and design studio, and Disney. He started at the Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) in 2019, and after finishing the major project of reviving the worm logotype, retired in 1992, he has worked full-time at NASA headquarters since 2023.

blocks.cap: 'The Meatball' (left) and 'The Worm' (right)

blocks.x: In 1992, a newly arrived administrator disliked the worm and brought back 'the Meatball,' the Apollo-era insignia. Rager says that for a while, part of his job was writing a 'peace treaty' between the two logos. The worm's designer, now in his 90s, never expected to see the logo again, but it has since become a permanent part of the Museum of Modern Art's (MoMA) collection.

An old brand can easily start to look like wallpaper to the people inside it. That's why Rager spends a lot of time training internal teams on the brand's values and what consistent communication means. NASA isn't selling a product, he says, but optimism and humanity, and since it runs on taxpayer money, it has to show that investment is worth it.

blocks.cap: A page from NASA's 1975 brand guidelines

blocks.x: On the question of trust in an age of AI and misinformation, his answer is clear: "I've banned the use of AI imagery." Tech-savvy staff pushed back hard, but he stressed that NASA's brand stands on trust. People need to know that when they see a NASA image, it's real and can be believed at face value, because there are already plenty of people looking for excuses not to believe something.

NASA's communications manifesto requires using what actually exists first. As Rager puts it: "We have an abundance of great imagery, artwork, and amazing photography. We already have the kind of material AI wants to create."

Corel has added Text-to-Vector to the CorelDRAW Graphics Suite's September 2026 update. The AI introduced earlier this year wasn't vector-based, but this tool is different. It generates vector artwork from text prompts or reference material such as illustrations, logos, product designs, and photos, and hands over the result as objects, curves, and nodes. Colors, shapes, and individual elements can be edited afterward, just like a hand-drawn piece.

blocks.cap: You can feed in your own work as a reference and use Text-to-Vector to generate more editable assets. (Image: Corel)

blocks.x: In a demo by Jenny John, who handles CorelDRAW product management, what stood out was the reference workflow rather than simple prompting. When an illustration by artist Pawel Pergol (around 600 objects) was fed in and the tool was asked to make rabbit, bird, and snake icons in the same style, the result opened in the objects panel, down to editable curves and nodes. John said, "That's exactly where the artist's work begins." Beta testers mostly used it to generate new pieces from existing logos and illustrations.

There are three models. Vector Spark handles simple work like icons and clip art, Vector Craft is general-purpose, and Vector Master covers complex designs and reference-based variations. There's no guarantee every detail of a reference image survives, so some manual fixing remains. According to John, beta artists are picky about tracing-type work but "really love" the AI for idea generation.

blocks.cap: (Image: Corel)

blocks.x: PowerTRACE was also reworked. Tracing is up to four times faster, object structure and color handling have improved, and AI background removal has been added. The generation features run in the cloud, not on a graphics card; a local AI running on GPUs like Nvidia's is not on the roadmap. Text-to-Vector is also coming to CorelDRAW Go and CorelDRAW Technical Suite 2026.
CorelDRAW Graphics Suite costs $269 (£319) a year, or $549 (£659) for a perpetual license. To mark the launch, unlimited Vector Craft and Vector Master generations are offered for free for one week.

On September 25, 2026, UserTesting announced Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers for its own platform and for User Interviews. Product, design, UX, and research teams can recruit participants, build studies, launch tests, and even receive feedback from inside MCP-compatible AI apps such as ChatGPT, Claude, Figma Make, and Gemini. According to MarTech Series, this is currently in early access, and the combined participant network of the two services spans more than 7 million people across 34 countries.

UserTesting's argument runs like this: AI can produce concepts quickly, but the results keep gravitating toward the familiar. Building a genuinely distinctive product requires real human emotion and judgment.

iFynx, who wrote the piece, recommends placing 'research gates' in agent workflows — requiring a set number of target-market sessions after an information architecture (IA) proposal, after a microcopy draft, and after designing high-risk screens like payment confirmation, before an agent can mark a ticket 'ready for development.' Without such a process, studies get launched indiscriminately, results get skimmed over, and sensitive prototype copy can leak out to the wrong participant pool.

iFynx's conclusion is that MCP is just plumbing — governance is the real product. Teams need to decide first who can launch a paid study from an agent session, and what kinds of personal information should never go into a prompt. The flow from prototyping to testing to revision in Figma Make should also be one continuous process, not three tools that lose context between them. The piece also advises that for the Middle East and North Africa (MENA) market, studies should always include users of Gulf dialects and Egyptian Arabic, as well as users on lower- and mid-tier Android devices.

It looks like Google is preparing yet another update to its image model, Nano Banana. A Google Flow web build originally showed the label 'Nano Banana 2.5 Flash,' but that name has now simply changed to 'Nano Banana 2.1.'

The name change suggests Nano Banana 2.1 could be the official product name. Still, it's worth tempering expectations about the scope of the upgrade — going from 2 to 2.1 is usually an incremental improvement, a far cry from the leap that '2.5 Flash' implied.

If it ships under this name, Nano Banana 2.1 could land across several Google products, including Gemini, Google AI Studio, and Google Flow, which would also fit how Google rolls out releases these days. Nano Banana 2's official name is Gemini 3.1 Flash Image, and Nano Banana 2 Lite has already been deployed to both developer-facing and consumer services.

No release timeline has surfaced for Nano Banana 2.1, and Google hasn't disclosed what changes from Nano Banana 2. Creators and developers want to know one thing: whether there's a noticeable improvement in generation quality, editing, consistency, and latency — or just a new checkpoint swapped in.

Attention is also shifting toward Google's next-generation Gemini Pro. Google hasn't announced a release date for Gemini 4 Pro, but TestingCatalog expects the next Pro-tier model to arrive before December.

If a human operator can't tell what an AI agent is thinking in real time, that agent isn't useful. The writer's team built a React dashboard that shows the agent's reasoning, memory hits, and recovery actions, and operator trust shifted noticeably.

The first UI was a simple table listing incidents. It showed what happened but not why. Operators couldn't tell whether the agent had pulled from Hindsight memory or reasoned fresh with an LLM. Internal survey trust scored 2 out of 10. When confidence isn't visible, operators override the call — and if they're going to override it every time, there's no point having an agent.

The fix was to expose the reasoning. The MemoryHitBadge component marks the source of every solution with one of two colors: purple for a direct pull from Hindsight memory (zero LLM tokens), orange for fresh ReAct reasoning that then gets saved to memory as a playbook. The badge also shows elapsed time and a confidence percentage.

A real-time topology graph built with @xyflow/react was added too. It keeps the whole microservice structure and status on screen, and when an incident hits, the affected services light up — no need to dig through logs to see the blast radius.

The dashboard polls a BFF (Backend-For-Frontend) every three seconds. A single TanStack Query setting, refetchIntervalInBackground: false, stops polling when a tab is inactive, dropping background traffic to near zero when nobody's watching. In the team's testing, render latency fell from 2.5 seconds to 150ms, and operator trust rose from 2 to 8. The number of UI pages grew from 1 to 11.

A confidence badge reads faster than a log file, and a topology diagram reads faster than a metrics dump. That's why the writer says anyone building an AI agent should budget plenty of engineering time for the UI — it isn't decoration, it's where the agent's reasoning meets human judgment.

AI and animation together tend to split opinion. With job and copyright worries recurring, animation in particular has pushed back hard against AI. When artist Antrofrog's AI animation recently went viral, the hostility didn't let up either. The mix of oddly familiar styles and a strange plot made viewers quickly recognize it as AI work, and they aired their complaints without hesitation.

A tall man carrying an umbrella moves through the city to Sade's 'Smooth Operator.' He catches a falling flowerpot from a window and rescues a cat stuck in a tree, his expression flat throughout. At first glance it's playful and harmless, but look closer and cracks appear. The art style itself is inconsistent: the protagonist looks like a Japanese anime villain dropped into a classic Disney film, while background characters mix storybook illustration with old New Yorker cartoons.

blocks.cap: The umbrella-carrying man and a child holding ice cream, from the animation Antrofrog posted on X. (Image: Antrofrog via X)

blocks.x: Accusations of stolen character designs followed. One comment pointed at the boy holding ice cream and asked, "Isn't that Ben from 'Song of the Sea'?" The plot also came under fire. The protagonist knocks a kid on a scooter into the street and even ruins a stranger's painting. One X user remarked, "There's basically no storytelling fundamentals here at all."

blocks.cap: Two men in suits appear in Antrofrog's AI animation. (Image: Antrofrog via X)

blocks.x: There was also this reaction: "The tragedy of AI art isn't that it looks ugly — it's that it makes you distrust people." Once you start questioning whether a gesture, a pace, or a pause was intentional or just a hallucination from a probability calculation, the immersion breaks. As the tools get more sophisticated and easier to use, more voices are asking what counts as human creativity, and whether prompt-made work belongs on the same stage as human-made work.

blocks.cap: Selecting only part of an image, then refining the result with hue and saturation controls.

blocks.x: Adobe has added interactive editing to its Adobe plugin for ChatGPT, timed to OpenAI's DevDay 2026 announcement. Users can now directly touch up images, designs, and PDFs.

The approach: select part of an image, hand the edit to ChatGPT, then fine-tune the result with new controls. Moving between the editor and the conversation doesn't break the work's context. The editor appears in a ChatGPT side panel and surfaces only the controls that match the edit you're making. Say you want to change an object's color, and a color control appears that applies only to that selection.

Vibhor Chhabra, OpenAI's product lead for the ChatGPT ecosystem, said, "We want people to go from an idea straight to something they can use or share, while still being able to hold onto the details along the way."

The image and design editor runs on Photoshop and Adobe Express. Select an object or paint over it with a brush to touch up just that part, then use sliders to adjust hue, saturation, and contrast. If a napkin ends up in a latte photo meant for social media, paint over the napkin with the brush and say, "remove the napkin from the table." Then paint the cup again and ask for brightness and contrast adjustments, and two sliders appear right away.

blocks.cap: Conversation and direct editing move back and forth inside ChatGPT.

blocks.x: Whatever gets touched up in the editor carries back into the conversation as context. There's no need to re-explain the task or re-upload the file. Switch to conversation when speed matters, and to direct manipulation when precision does.

blocks.cap: Acrobat tools let you fix PDF text right inside the document.

blocks.x: PDFs are handled by Acrobat tools. Open a document in the side panel, fix text, and highlight passages. Highlight the payment-terms paragraph in a freelance contract and ask it to find more sections about billing and payments, and Acrobat marks those passages in the document.
Adobe recently combined its creative and productivity tools into a single plugin across ChatGPT, Claude, and Slack. This update rolls out worldwide starting today on ChatGPT web and app, in stages.
Anthropic unveiled Claude Sonnet 5.5 on September 28, the second model in the Claude 5.5 lineup. It is a clear step up from Sonnet 5, more than 30% faster, and up to 30% cheaper for most tasks.

Sonnet 5.5 is the faster, cheaper model that supports Opus 5.5. While Opus 5.5 handles complex work that needs careful judgment, Sonnet 5.5 is strongest at everyday tasks with clear scope, bug fixes, and producing polished documents, slides, and spreadsheets. Anthropic also describes it as having "a sharp eye for design." Claude Haiku 5.5, built for high-volume, low-cost use, joins the lineup in a few weeks.

The performance gap is large. It scored 70.6% on Terminal-Bench 4.0, an agentic coding evaluation, versus 10.3% for Sonnet 5. On GDPval-AA it fell only 2 points short of Opus 5.5, and it's the first Sonnet model to beat Pokémon Red using only screenshots.

Pricing is unchanged from Sonnet 5: $2 per million input tokens, $10 per million output tokens, and $0.20 for cache reads. Because it finishes the same work in far fewer tokens, the cost per task has dropped by up to 30%.

blocks.cap: Sonnet 5.5's output for the prompt, "a murmuration of 400 starlings in a single HTML file."

blocks.x: Early testers singled out its design sense. They say it adds polish to user interfaces and produces slide decks that need almost no touch-up beyond the template. In internal testing, given a public company's quarterly earnings materials, a call transcript, and a slide template, and asked to produce a 10-page operating review, two experts judged the first draft good enough to send as is.
Its cybersecurity capability is now close to Opus 5, and it's the first Sonnet model to ship with the same cyber safeguards as the flagship models.

This is advice for people who vibe code. The author, Maya Brennan, says she has landed on three conclusions amid today's flood of AI slop: people can spot slop, they dislike it, but they don't know how to fix it. Recognizing bad design and fixing it are entirely different skills.

That doesn't mean every AI output is slop. Most interfaces today are built at least partly through vibe coding, and AI has also produced plenty of expressive design. Slop is output made with no thought, effort, or quality, usually churned out at volume. It skips considered decisions, piles on clutter, and tells every story the same way.

The first step is analysis. Instead of stopping at "it just looks off," you need to pin down exactly which elements make something look like slop. The author includes a cheat sheet of "slop signals" to watch for in vibe-coded UI.

blocks.cap: Slop signals that show up in vibe-coded UI.

blocks.x: Removing it happens in stages. Level 0 is a one-line prompt. Ask for a Y2K slide deck for trivia night with no reference style, and the slop signals come through fully intact. Asking it to look "less vibe-coded" doesn't do much either.

Level 1 is cleanup: strip out unnecessary elements and specify color, font, and graphics explicitly. Even just using a Coolors palette, Google Fonts, and Lucide icons makes an interface noticeably more polished, and adding Unsplash photos gives it an analog feel.

blocks.cap: A slide regenerated after specifying a font and palette.

blocks.x: Level 2 is setting an aesthetic: attach reference images or describe a style in words. AI is weak with organic, expressive styles and reproduces "digital" styles better. The author does draw one line, though — don't feed in someone else's work without permission just to have it copied.

Level 3 is real design. For something as large as a website, draw inspiration from Dribbble and Mobbin, sketch wireframes by hand, build the frames yourself in Figma, and then use that design as the standard the AI implementation has to meet.

blocks.cap: The result of having it faithfully reproduce a Figma file.

blocks.x: These stages are meant for one-off designs. For a whole product or brand, you also need to bring in agent workflows and a design system.

OpenAI unveiled a new AI agent product line called "Dots." They look like something straight out of a children's cartoon. Dots was the centerpiece among roughly 20 announcements at the fourth DevDay, held September 29 in San Francisco. Dots are always-on agents running on the latest model, GPT-6 Astra.
Dots don't follow OpenAI's signature "Void" logo. Instead, each one wears its own cute, soft-edged character — a bow-tied triangle, a rabbit in headphones, a cloud in a beret.

Each Dot uses its own cloud computer, learns from feedback, and connects to more than 4,000 apps through a plugin ecosystem. You can ask it questions and give it feedback the way you would a coworker, in ChatGPT, Slack, or Teams, and voice calls work too.
Users first name their main Dot and style it to fit how they'll use it. Examples shown included Todd, a chubby, smiling frog; Jojo, a heart wearing sunglasses; and Felipe, a soft blue cloud.

Fast Company doesn't see the cuteness as accidental. It comes at a moment when anxiety about AI agents is especially high. Just as Meta rolled out its anthropomorphized Muse agent earlier this month, the analysis suggests OpenAI is also leaning heavily on character design to address trust concerns.
Meta is bringing its long-promised photorealistic avatar within a few months. It's called "Hologram." Road to VR's Scott Hayden tried it in person at Meta Connect.

Hologram debuts first in Meta Ray-Ban Display, which has a single transparent display over the right eye. It was previously called "Codec Avatars." It's also coming to the newly announced Meta VR glasses, but that version doesn't launch until spring 2027.

Strictly speaking, it's not a 3D lightfield hologram. It's an AI-infused immersive avatar, closer to 2.5D. The creation process also differs from Apple's Persona. Instead of scanning your face with a Vision Pro sensor, you follow a few prompts using the Meta mobile app and the selfie camera — answering what your favorite day is on the spot, reading a short sentence while smiling, and turning your head side to side.

The display version moves using voice alone, so AI does a lot of the work. It's rolling out first in the US, in early access limited to WhatsApp video calls. The author's avatar wasn't identical to him, but it could fool someone who didn't know him.

It's a different story with the VR glasses. Sensors on the bottom of the headset track your eyes and face, and the avatar appears full-body, head to toe. It has a sense of dimension but not real depth, so you can't walk around a room or fist-bump in it. Hand poses, hair, and shirt movement are all generated by AI.

So is it better than Apple's Persona? The author says it depends on what you mean by "better." Persona is still a floating head, but it has real 3D depth, and Vision Pro's face tracking is eerily accurate.

Maxon has released Cinema 4D 2026.4, a new version of its 3D software for motion graphics, VFX and visualization. The update's core feature is a new MCP server. It lets external AI tools such as Claude or ChatGPT run repetitive tasks automatically.

An MCP (Model Context Protocol) server opens an app's features to external AI tools. The Cinema 4D MCP server officially supports Claude Desktop and ChatGPT Desktop, and runs the program through natural-language prompts. Maxon describes it as a way to offload procedural, repetitive work without breaking the creative flow.

Cited uses include changing scene hierarchies or naming conventions, managing multi-pass renders, and setting up camera tracking. It can also handle basic modeling, UV editing, character rigging and animation, and particle and fluid simulations, with more complex tasks left to Python scripts.

blocks.cap: A 3D environment assembled from off-the-shelf assets while conversing with an AI agent.

blocks.x: Still, mindful of users wary of AI, Maxon's documentation stresses that the feature is not a generative system. "It doesn't invent designs, doesn't generate images, and has no opinion on whether a shot looks good. It has no taste. Every instruction comes from the user, every action stays in the undo list, and turning off the MCP server means nothing happens."

The server runs locally on the artist's computer and is off by default. Using it with other devices on the local network requires separate permission. It also connects to apps that run AI models locally, like LM Studio, though GPU memory can be a bottleneck. It only works in the full version of Cinema 4D, not the Lite edition bundled with After Effects, Team Render, or command-line rendering.

Cinema 4D joins DaVinci Resolve and Unreal Engine, which added MCP servers earlier this year. Blender has an official MCP server as an add-on, and Houdini showed a technical preview in Houdini 22. Cinema 4D 2026.4 runs on Windows 10 or later and macOS 14.0 or later, and is sold only by subscription: $109 a month or $839 a year.

blocks.cap: A screen in Photoshop beta where a light has been added with a Relight layer.

blocks.x: Adobe has added Relight, a generative AI feature, to desktop Photoshop beta. It lets you add new, interactive, non-destructive lighting to an image, effectively relighting a shot after it's already taken. You move the light source, change its intensity, color and diffusion, and watch the result update in real time.

Relight erases an image's existing lighting, then creates new lighting with generative AI. You can add up to three artificial light sources and adjust each one separately. Turning all of them off leaves only ambient or original light, and switching each source on and off works like real lighting.

Early experiments posted on social media have drawn mixed reactions. Some say it could replace manual light painting, or at least give a strong starting point that speeds up the work considerably. Others say the texture gets mushy, making the result look more like a 3D avatar than a realistic portrait. Like other AI editing tools, it also tends to change a person's features in unintended ways. The same debate that surrounded Nvidia's DLSS 5, over whether it preserves the original or generates a new picture, is repeating itself here.

The unnatural look can be reduced by using Relight like an adjustment layer and hand-blending the result to bring back the original texture. It's still a feature that just launched in beta, so it's likely to be refined before the full release.

To use it, update to the latest beta build (Version: 27.10.0 202600802.m.3625), open an image, and choose New Relight layer from the Layer menu. A default white light appears in the center of the screen, which you can drag inside or outside the canvas. A separate 'Relight Layer' appears in the Layers panel, leaving the original pixels untouched. Pressing 'Done' after adjusting produces the final result at the original resolution. Each time you press Done, though, it costs 30 credits.

blocks.cap: Image from the Runway Ads announcement.

blocks.x: Runway announced Runway Ads, a new product that runs and optimizes the creative side of paid advertising from start to finish. Connect it to an ad account and brand kit, and it produces video and image creative, then publishes approved variants directly to Meta, Google and TikTok. It reads performance back from the same platforms and makes the next round of creative based on what actually pulled in budget.

Performance advertising rewards volume. But most advertisers put real budget behind only a fraction of the ads they make. Without constant iteration and steady execution, you don't extract the full value available from a running program. Finding what works has less to do with taste or judgment than with how many variants a team can produce. Regardless of size, what holds a company back isn't analysis or intuition but the capacity to produce enough creative.

Runway Ads solves this by combining the process of creating, watching and fixing performance ad campaigns into one. For large companies running global campaigns at scale, testing gets faster, variation increases and localization stays consistent. Small teams can also run thousands of ads a week and shift toward what's working every day. Small businesses and individual creators get into new channels without taking time away from their core work.
Runway Ads automates the key steps of ad generation and buying, building on Runway's agent work, while leaving ownership and approval with people.

Runway built the product on the infrastructure it used to grow its own performance marketing, especially on Meta and TikTok ads. Since July, its weekly ad count grew from 77 to roughly 900, and return on ad spend doubled. Conversion rate rose about 34% while click-through rate stayed flat. Even as spending rose to scale up, cost per subscriber fell 41% over the same period.

Runway co-CEO Anastasis Germanidis said, "We built Runway Ads because we needed it ourselves." He added that, "instead of stitching together three separate tools for creating, publishing and measuring ads, putting it all in one system made our paid ad efficiency visible at a glance, and let us move faster and try more to take market share."
Runway is piloting Runway Ads with select enterprise partners. Enterprise sales will reach out to advertisers who share their paid ad program.

blocks.cap: A planetary gearbox made with OwlCAD.

blocks.x: Spare Matter Corp has released OwlCAD, a parametric CAD program for 3D printing, in beta. It runs entirely in the browser, so there's nothing to install and no account needed. The geometry engine processes the model on the user's own computer, so there's no waiting on server responses. The full editor, including every export format, is free, and there's no license fee even if you sell the prints or files. AI features and agent access through the MCP server are part of the Pro plan, at $12 a month or $120 a year.

AI 3D generators have been producing plausible-looking shapes on screen for a while now. The problem shows up when you need to widen a hole by 0.4mm. A triangle mesh doesn't remember that it was ever a hole. OwlCAD offers something more modest but practical: a model with live dimensions and a preserved edit history.

blocks.cap: The editor screen, where dimensions can be edited directly.

blocks.x: Describe a part in words, and parametric mode returns a node tree built from basic solids, boolean operations and transforms, with every dimension still editable. Change 30mm to 32mm and the whole part regenerates, and like any other edit, it can be undone. Edits made through the Modify with AI feature don't bake into the geometry either, they're added to the model's history. The company's own explanation is simple: a mesh remembers what something looks like; a parametric model remembers how it was built.

Underneath the AI is a full editor. It uses constraint-based sketching, extrude/revolve/sweep/loft, per-edge fillets and chamfers, assemblies with mates and a BOM, variables and formulas, and 33 generators covering gears, threads, hinges, enclosures and Gridfinity bins, among others. For printing, it adds custom tolerance presets, overhang/thin-wall/watertightness checks, printer profiles, automatic orientation, and mass and cost estimates.

blocks.cap: A screen checking overhangs and wall thickness before printing.

blocks.x: With the hosted MCP server, MCP clients that talk over HTTP, such as Claude Code, Claude Desktop and Cursor, can build and fix models without a CAD app. With 29 tools, an agent assembles the model tree, renders a preview to review its own work, checks overhangs and print volume, and calculates filament use and cost. A large part can also be split into two pieces joined with dowels, slots, locating pins or screws. In a benchmark the company published, Gemini 3.6 Flash built and validated an 80×60×5mm mounting plate with four holes, then estimated it would use 18.5g of PLA.

blocks.cap: A design workbench with sketches and models.

blocks.x: Professor Steven Pum, who has taught at Parsons School of Design for nearly 30 years, long located a young designer's value in technical skill: drawing, making, rendering, prototyping, and learning new digital tools. Now, a few minutes can produce polished images, presentations, and even a visual direction. When production becomes common, something else becomes scarce.

He sees the competitive edge as having moved upstream. A beautiful image is no longer scarce; knowing which image is worth making has become what matters. Before making a chair, a designer decides whether that chair is needed, who will use it, and what it should communicate. AI can help with the making, but it can't take responsibility for the decision. That's why a portfolio often reveals more through failed experiments, abandoned concepts, and the thinking behind them than through finished work.

The research results are mixed. A 2025 study of 5,172 customer service agents found that generative AI assistance raised productivity by an average of 15%, with bigger gains for less experienced people. By contrast, a 2024 experiment with 60 participants found that those using an AI image generator showed more design fixation, with lower counts, diversity and originality of ideas across the board. In a 2025 field experiment with 250 employees at a technology consulting firm, AI's creative benefit stood out most among people with strong metacognitive strategies.

Pum isn't arguing for separating designers from AI, but for carefully deciding when AI enters the process. When reviewing work, he asks which problem was chosen and which alternatives were dropped, and why. Before bringing in AI, he gives time to observe customers and context so the problem can be defined independently. For a request to improve hospital wayfinding signage, that means asking why patients get lost before pulling up drafts. The friction that builds expertise is sometimes worth protecting.

He pictures the designer of the future not as someone who knows every AI tool, but as someone who knows when to use it, what to ask, what to doubt, and when not to use it at all. A designer who produces 100 concepts an hour may be more productive. A designer who notices that 99 of them are solving the wrong problem may be more valuable. His conclusion is that organizations, too, should evaluate problem definition and judgment and experimentation, not just speed, volume and polish.
Figma가 'Release Notes 2026: September Edition'에서 Figma Motion의 새 기능과 캔버스 업데이트를 소개했다.
Motion은 이제 디자인 시스템용 맞춤 애니메이션 스타일과 오디오, 텍스트 애니메이션을 지원한다. Figma 에이전트, 그리고 MCP로 연결한 코딩 에이전트가 이 기능을 자동으로 적용할 수 있고 Lottie로 곧장 내보낼 수도 있다.
Community Riffs도 공개됐다. 애니메이션과 프로토타입, 실험작을 Figma Community 페이지에 바로 공유할 수 있다. 코드 뷰어와 MCP가 업데이트돼 에이전트와 함께 고친 내용을 다시 Figma로 보내는 것도 가능해졌다.
세션에서는 런치 애니메이션과 텍스트 스태거, 키프레임 이징, 마케팅 에셋 자동 스케일링, 생성형 플러그인과 셰이더, 캔버스 안의 맞춤 AI 스킬, Weave의 이미지 생성, 변수로 쓰는 불투명도, 디자인-코드 충실도 개선까지 보여준다.
CSS's border-image is a feature people know about but tend to pass over. In short, it uses an image or gradient as the border instead of plain lines like solid or dashed.

There's one big catch: a border image doesn't bend to follow the border's shape. Even so, the author likes border-image for its efficiency. It gets cropped well and applies itself to all four sides automatically. That trait pays off especially when animating border images and gradients.

The example is nothing fancy: a single div with some formatted text. After setting a size for .card and laying down a background image, the text is tweaked slightly so it doesn't sit flush on top of the background.

A solid-color CSS gradient is used for the border, for two reasons. A gradient is also a type of background image, and it's convenient for showing animation. The gradient is placed where the border goes using border-image-source, border-image-slice, and border-image-width. In the demo, there's a small gap between the moving border and the image.

Here's the catch: gradients don't animate by default. So the author registers a custom property directly, since CSS variables can animate. Register a variable like --p with a syntax type such as <percentage>, <angle>, or <number>, apply a transition on hover, and the border moves.

There's no reason to stop here. Use conic-gradient instead of linear-gradient, animate the border-image-slice value itself, and set border-image-repeat to round so it tiles like a repeating pattern. Moving the slice from 1 to 20 pixels on hover makes the border pattern break apart choppily. It's not a technique a coding agent would come up with on its own.

This is a video in which Figma walks through how agents work inside a design file. Support for FigJam and Slides was announced as coming next. It's the clearest statement yet, in the company's own words, that agents aren't replacing existing files but settling inside them.

Getting started is simple. Pick a layer on the canvas and click Agents, and a prompt box appears on the canvas. The shortcut is Cmd or Ctrl + Enter. Clicking Agents in the left navigation keeps the sidebar open and continues the conversation.

Figma describes the agent's role in three parts: creating and varying designs, automating busywork, and getting design feedback. Prompts can produce new screens and layouts, and adjust layout, spacing, and component instances. They apply existing styles and variables and create or edit images. The list also includes writing and editing bulk content, building plugins and shaders, adding motion and animation, and connecting design libraries.

What it can't do is clear too. Vector editing and the Draw tool are still in progress, and it cannot export assets or create diagrams and data visualizations. It also can't be used on mobile or in other Figma products.

There's no plan restriction. However, you need a Full seat with edit permission to actually change the file; View, Dev, or Collab seats can only chat. It's open for free during the beta, but with a monthly usage cap that resets each month.

blocks.cap: MableLink.

blocks.x: Mohamed Ragheb's MableLink is a pipeline connector made with Maya users specifically in mind. Instead of flattening a scene down to a plain export, it keeps the underlying data intact.

It sends animated Maya scenes straight to Blender and Unreal while preserving rigs, animation, blend shapes, cameras, lights, pivots, and hierarchy. Physically based materials like glass, subsurface scattering, emission, and clearcoat come along too. It also supports live re-sync with Blender and Unreal, NURBS, GLB/GLTF import and export with smart texture compression, operation without a Blender dependency, and mesh-to-voxel conversion for MagicaVoxel.
There are two versions. The free version gives 20 transfers to Blender, 20 to Unreal, and 5 physically based material transfers. Pro removes these limits and adds Update Sync.

Installation takes just a few minutes. Drag and drop it into Maya, click once in Blender, and run a single script in Unreal, and it installs as a real plugin across every project in that engine. It also carries over to projects created later. A portable .mable package bundles the scene, materials, and textures into one file so anyone on the team can open it in Blender or Unreal.
Compatibility covers Maya 2024/2027, Blender 4.5 LTS/5.2 LTS, and Unreal Engine 5.8. Work on it is still ongoing, and it recently moved from v0.1 to v0.1.3.
Pro is a one-time purchase. The same license key works on up to 5 devices, and it stays valid even after reinstalling.

blocks.cap: Autodesk Mudbox.

blocks.x: Autodesk is discontinuing Mudbox, its digital sculpting software. It was a tool used in concept art, game development, visual effects, and motion graphics.
Sales and renewals of the 3-year subscription already ended on August 7, 2026. Monthly and annual subscriptions follow on November 7, 2026.

Mudbox came out of Wētā FX 20 years ago. It was created by artists Andrew Camenisch, Dave Cardwell, and Tibor Madjar, who left the studio after working on King Kong in 2005. The three received a 2014 Academy technical award for “powerful new design features that significantly raised the state of the art for multi-resolution digital sculpting.” Autodesk acquired the original developer, Skymatter, in 2007.

Around 2017, Autodesk invested again and added a dynamic tessellation system in Mudbox 2018.2. Noticeable improvements stopped there. Mudbox 2027, released in March 2026, was “the sixth consecutive annual update with no new features listed in its release notes.”

Even with no new features for years, artists kept their roughly $105-a-year subscriptions. The reason was its intuitive, layer-based workflow. Unlike ZBrush or 3DCoat, whose interfaces and workflows depart from the norm, Mudbox never felt unfamiliar to people coming from other CG software.

blocks.cap: A fan recreation of Disney's Princess Merida, sculpted in Mudbox by character artist Xhon Hysenaj. It served as the last promotional image on Autodesk's Mudbox website.

blocks.x: Subscribers as of August 7, 2026 will be able to use Mudbox 2027 for five years. Technical support and security patches, however, run only for three years, after which there will be no new features or bug fixes.

Anyone who has built something with Claude or Cursor lately knows the pattern. The code is clean and the logic holds up, but the screen looks like a 2015-era Bootstrap clone. Every corner is rounded the same way, shadows get slapped on without conveying any depth, and the animations feel robotic rather than organic.

Agents are good at producing working HTML and CSS, but they have no concept of design intent. They can write code that paints a button blue, but they don't know why a spring scale should kick in on press, or how elevation should shift against the background plane. The result is a “zombie” interface: it works, but it has no life, and that is a technical problem that touches accessibility and user control as well.

The tool he uses to close that gap is the UI/UX Excellence Prover, attached via Vinkius. It doesn't write code for him; instead, it acts as a design unit test wired into the agent pipeline, checking whether a generated component meets 2026 standards across six pillars.

The first flag is “flat decoration.” Agents slap a box-shadow on every card because it looks modern, but a shadow is meant to signal space, not decorate. A well-built screen expresses hierarchy through elevation levels from 0 to 5; shadow everything and nothing stands out anymore. The Prover catches unjustified shadows and forces elevation to be defined with tokens that actually mean depth.

Motion is no different. LLM output leans on transition: ease-in-out. Page transitions should follow the direction of movement, and a click needs more than a color change—it needs a spring scale that mimics touch. The Prover looks for motion tokens with set durations and physical properties instead of arbitrary millisecond values, and flags any movement that doesn't serve explanation, guidance, or confirmation as clutter.

The place this breaks down most is state design. It's easy to think only of default and click, but a real product needs at least eight: Idle, Hover, Active/Pressed, Focus-visible, Disabled, Loading, Success, Error. A button missing loading or error feedback is technical debt by itself, and the Prover finds the missing states and makes them get implemented.

The accessibility check targets “accessibility theater.” Plenty of sites claim WCAG 2.2 AA compliance while icon buttons go without an aria-label or the focus ring is broken. The Prover checks against WCAG 2.2 AAA: contrast of at least 4.5:1, a properly working focus-visible state, and a prefers-reduced-motion fallback.

It also looks at dark patterns. The “calm UI” the Prover enforces checks whether irreversible actions like deletion carry deliberate friction, and whether pre-checked boxes or hidden cancellation paths are absent.

Connecting is simple for any MCP-supporting client: just drop a Vinkius token into Cursor or Claude Desktop. Rather than asking the AI to be creative, it means sitting a verifier next to it that states flatly that there must be eight states, that motion must use spring physics, that spacing must follow an 8px grid. Design moves from a subjective conversation to a verifiable engineering requirement.
This is a video posted by Figma's official channel, 「How Figma made copy + paste faster」. True to its title, it walks through the engineering work that made copy and paste much faster.

Copy and paste is the least flashy but most-used action in a design tool. It's a reminder that how polished a tool feels often comes down to unglamorous latency work nobody presents, more than any visible visual finish.

blocks.cap: Makera's ecosystem of CNC software, mobile control, and project sharing.

blocks.x: Makera has released Makera Studio, Makerables, and the Makera app. It is an ecosystem aimed at desktop CNC users that brings software and community together, built to work across Makera's desktop CNC lineup, including the Carvera, Carvera Air, and Z1.

CAM software, project sharing, and mobile machine control all enter a single flow. It supports the steps of finding a project, preparing files, machining, learning, and sharing again, which cuts down on the separate tools needed when moving between software, community material, and machine operation.

Makera Studio is an integrated platform that puts CAM, machining simulation, and machine control into one workspace. It covers manufacturing steps from loading a model, choosing a machining strategy, generating toolpaths, previewing results, through to operating the machine. For tasks like 2D/3D machining, 3-axis/4-axis relief carving, and laser engraving, Guided Modes help first-time users set up a project, with automatic parameter optimization for common materials and machining simulation to check the work before cutting.

Makerables is a community platform for CNC creators. It includes AI-assisted tools that generate designs from text prompts, existing images, or initial concepts. It is also where reference images get turned into reliefs or 3D models, and where projects get refined for CNC production. Projects can hold design files, CAM data, machining programs, material recommendations, tool information, machining parameters, documentation, and assembly notes.

Users can browse projects, upload their own work, and exchange feedback with other makers, then continue editing or machining directly in Makera Studio. Makera has also launched a Co-Creation Contest that gives selected contributors recommendations, editorial features, community events, and exposure opportunities.

The Makera app moves part of the Studio and Makerables flow to mobile. From a smartphone, users can connect to and control a Makera machine, and browse recommended projects and community work through the Makerables integration. Advanced features like AI content generation or project publishing stay on desktop, while the app focuses on project browsing and machine control.

Makerables is open to makers worldwide, while Makera Studio is used by Makera customers. By layering CAM software, AI-assisted creation, and a maker community on top of the hardware, the scope of the desktop CNC product has widened.

blocks.cap: Photoshop 27.9.1, as released by Adobe.

blocks.x: Adobe has released Photoshop 27.9.1, the latest version of the image editing program used for concept art, texture editing, and render retouching.

It's a workflow update at heart. The AI-powered Generate Image and Remove tools got refined, and a feature for saving a list of favorite fonts was added. A critical bug in 27.9 itself has also been fixed this time.

You might wonder why Photoshop jumped straight from 27.8 to 27.9.1, and CG Channel wondered the same thing. According to users on the Photoshop subreddit, 27.9 came out in late July but was pulled quickly over a bug that made images look faded. Photoshop product manager Cory Shubert wrote on the bug report forum that 27.9.1 fixed this issue, which is why the version in the release notes is 27.9.1.

Aside from the bug fix, this release mostly refines the workflow.
