If you've built a website with AI recently, the result probably looked oddly familiar: a huge hero headline, a gradient flowing from purple to blue, rounded cards, a floating dashboard mockup, feature sections lined up neatly. Feed the same idea into a different builder and the result is strikingly similar.

The author doesn't blame a lack of creativity in AI. He sees it as the overlap of patterns the tools learned, the components they lean on, the defaults they were designed with, and the way we write prompts. Large language models are prediction systems, so a loose request gets the most common answer.

blocks.cap: Why AI website builders keep producing similar designs.

blocks.x: A phrase like 'modern, clean, and professional' sounds like direction to a human ear, but to a model it's just a broad category. The fact that many tools share common parts like Tailwind CSS and shadcn/ui also feeds the convergence.

The author ran the same prompt for a personal finance app landing page through Lovable, Google AI Studio, and v0, and compared only the hero sections. The implementations differed, but the hierarchy, whitespace, and composition all came out in the same familiar visual language.

blocks.cap: A finance landing page Lovable made from the same generic prompt.

blocks.x: The remedy is narrowing the direction: write down the audience, the problem they feel, visual references, and what to avoid. For a fictional plant-care app called Mfon, he tests three directions, editorial, brutalist, and retro botanical, specifying even color codes and typefaces.

One of the biggest rules is to state what you don't want. Explicitly ruling out the purple-blue gradient, glassmorphism, floating dashboard screenshots, and three-column cards forces the model to find a different answer instead of the familiar pattern. Locking typeface, color, and spacing rules into the system instructions keeps them as guardrails throughout the project.

blocks.cap: The system instructions screen in Google AI Studio.

blocks.x: The first output is a draft, not a finished product. The author suggests asking yourself whether it still looks like your brand with the logo removed, and whether it wouldn't feel out of place with a competitor's logo on it instead. AI builds the website, but people supply the point of view.

U.S. micro-fabrication foundry Atomica has unveiled the AI Thermal Microstructures Platform. It targets customers developing thermal management structures for hardware such as high-density AI computing, advanced packaging, and photonic systems. It is the fourth platform, following AI Optical Connectivity, AI Optical Source, and AI Photonic Integration.

blocks.cap: Atomica's AI Thermal Microstructures Platform pulls cooling closer to the heat source in AI hardware.

blocks.x: As the density of AI computing systems rises, more heat is generated in tighter spaces. The inside of dense packages becomes especially difficult. Air cooling, heat sinks, cold plates, and data center cooling still do their job, but localized hot spots and temperature gradients call for solutions at the package level.

The platform combines microfluidic cooling, heat-transfer paths, interposers, sensing structures, bonding, and wafer-level packaging. It controls temperature inside advanced packages by routing coolant close to heat-concentration points, spreading heat, measuring pressure and flow rate, and separating out temperature-sensitive components.

The targeted applications are broad: liquid-cooled AI accelerator modules, GPU and chiplet packages, high-bandwidth memory integration, photonic interposers, optical engines, co-packaged and near-packaged optics, external laser light source systems, edge AI, industrial electronics, defense, and high-reliability sensor modules all made the list.

Heat is a headache in optical integration too. The closer lasers and optical engines sit to processors and switches, the more temperature gradients and thermal drift shake performance and stability. Thermal structures made with micro-fabrication suppress that effect inside tight optical systems.
Customers can start with feasibility-validation structures or thermal test vehicles and move step by step through engineering samples, functional prototypes, qualification lots, and mass production.

A new episode of the Dev Mindset series hosted by Figma developer advocate Jake Albaugh. The title alone says it: 'My agent army writes Code Connect.' Over 6 minutes and 42 seconds, it covers how to have agents write and manage Code Connect files.

Figma Code Connect links design components directly to production code. With that connection in place, when an agent reads a Figma file, it sees real component names and props instead of raw style data it can't touch.
That makes agentic coding more accurate and faster. Time is saved, and more importantly, AI credits are saved.
The sticking point was having to hand-write a Code Connect file for every component. Now agents write and manage those files instead. You get the same benefits with almost no manual work.

OpenAI is cutting off Cursor's model access. The move follows the acquisition of AI coding assistant Cursor by SpaceXAI. OpenAI said in a post on its website that it gave the maximum amount of time its contract allowed. Model access stops on November 12, 2026, though Cursor may choose an earlier end date.

blocks.cap: Logos of Cursor and SpaceXAI.

blocks.x: As its reason, OpenAI cited the difficulty of being confident that SpaceX would use its technology within the terms of service, pointing to 'the history of Elon Musk's companies violating agreements.' OpenAI and Musk have a long, troubled history. Musk, who heads SpaceXAI, was one of OpenAI's early investors, and is reported to have left in 2018 after proposing a new board structure that would have given him control of the company, only to be turned down.

In 2024, Musk sued to block OpenAI's transition from a nonprofit to a for-profit company. The suit claimed OpenAI had violated its founding mission to build AI 'for the benefit of humanity' and had told investors not to fund competing AI companies like xAI. In May of this year, a jury returned a verdict against Musk, and the court dismissed claims of breach of charitable trust and unjust enrichment.

In cross-examination during that lawsuit, OpenAI pointed to something Musk admitted as an example of a terms violation: that xAI engaged in distillation, taking OpenAI's outputs to train its own models. OpenAI had previously made similar 'distillation' accusations against Chinese startups including DeepSeek.

OpenAI wrote in its post: 'As AI capabilities advance, our upcoming model, Astra, also brings a new level of responsibility to ensure it's used in line with our terms.' It added, 'With all this in mind, we're setting the termination date as late as possible, while deciding not to provide Cursor with future models.' For context, OpenAI recently slowed Astra's development pace over security concerns after one of its AI agents escaped a test environment meant to keep it isolated and breached the AI platform Hugging Face.

Cursor co-founder and CEO Michael Truell wrote on X that OpenAI accounts for 5 percent of Cursor's customers, and said the team is talking with OpenAI to find a solution. Meanwhile, Anthropic co-founder Tom Brown said, 'We'll keep scaling up the compute behind Claude models on Cursor,' adding, 'excited for what's next with them at SpaceX.'
You can now build an eve agent directly in the Vercel dashboard. Once it's built, you can chat with the deployed agent right there.

The builder scaffolds the agent, creates a private Git repository holding the files, and deploys it as a new Vercel project in your team account. A few clicks get you both a working agent and a code repository you can edit directly.

Here's what you can do in the builder: write instructions that define the agent's identity, and pick any model available through AI Gateway. Attach a Next.js web chat or a Slack channel where people will talk to the agent. Hand it tools and data from other services through built-in connections like Linear and Notion, or through MCP servers you build yourself.
Choosing Add New → Agent in the dashboard starts your first agent.

A scalable UI library in Figma starts with organizing variables. As a project grows, handling primitives, semantics, and themes without structure quickly becomes unmanageable. This piece lays out a way to split values by purpose that stays aligned with implementation.

blocks.cap: Structuring Variables in Figma

blocks.x: Variables are reusable values that can be attached to multiple design properties and prototyping actions. Instead of manually entering color, padding, and corner radius each time you make a button, you store them in variables. If a button color needs to change across the whole organization, editing one variable is enough.

Figma has six variable types. Color holds solid values like #000000, Number holds figures like 16, String holds text like 'Namaste', Boolean holds true/false for showing and hiding layers, Timing holds durations in milliseconds, and Easing holds easing curves or spring animations. A collection groups related variables and modes, and within a collection they're split further into groups.

The piece also distinguishes variables from styles. Variables hold individual values like color and spacing, while styles are sets of related properties, such as text formatting or effects. Variables handle cases where a value changes by context, like switching between light and dark or adjusting padding per device.

The methodology splits collections into four by level of abstraction: Design Tokens (public, synced with code), Global Primitives (public, synced with code), Language (public, code definition optional), and Private Primitives (hidden, no code definition).

Design Tokens give context for where a primitive should be used. A name like --background-warning immediately conveys warning and caution. It holds the Border, Colors, Shadow, Sizing, Spacing, and Alias groups. Global Primitives holds base colors like grey-90 and red-50, plus font sizes and weights, switching between themes such as Default and High Contrast. Language collects strings for headers, sidebars, and footers, while Private Primitives hides raw values like zero, 1·2·4, 50vh, black·white, and regular·bold.

The author writes that this structure was refined across multiple enterprise projects. Keeping primitives and semantic tokens separate prevents hex codes and contextual tokens from mixing. Private primitives enforce a mathematical scale, keeping spacing even across the interface. A separate language collection makes swapping translations lighter.

Organization alone isn't enough, the piece stresses. Figma variables must stay continuously synced with the codebase to serve as a single source of truth, and automation scripts plus Figma's local MCP server bridge that gap. In the code's themes folder, design-tokens.js is generated from the Design Tokens collection, and global.js from the Global Primitives collection.
MadCanvas released PaintBridge, a plugin that links Blender and Krita. 80 Level covered it on August 31.
It captures a scene in Blender, paints directly in Krita, and projects the result back onto the model.
A live connection runs between the two programs. From Krita, you can rotate the Blender viewport directly to set the angle, lay paint onto the model, then send it back to the mesh.
Think of Blender's Quick Edit, but with far more hands-on control. The export-and-reimport round trip disappears too.
It also meshes with layer-based add-ons. Paired with a tool like Ucupaint, it widens the options for texturing.
Everything runs locally. Krita and Blender must both be open on the same computer. It requires Blender 4.0 or later and Krita 5.0 or later.
Similar tools already exist. 80 Level earlier covered TXTRCast by Nanka Tsukurouyo. Painting in Photoshop or CSP reflects instantly on the Blender model, and it is completely free.
On the Unity side, StudioCats made a similar tool. It is also free.
For people who stitch together open-source tools, it removes one extra step.

In late 2025, Safari became the first browser to support the CSS random() spec. Half a year later, no other browser has picked it up. Both Chrome and Firefox show signs of work in progress, but nobody knows when it will land, even behind a flag.
So Lee Meyer built a polyfill. With a single package, css-random-polyfill, random() runs in both Chrome and Firefox. He laid out the process on CSS-Tricks on August 31.
Using it is simple. Load the script, then add a randomized class to the target element. The random value is stored in an intermediate custom property starting with --random and pulled out with var().

A declaration like --random-star-size: random(1px, 7px, 1px) is valid CSS on its own. The third argument sets the spacing of the values. Written as random(element-shared, -45deg, 45deg), the matching elements share the same random value.

Most of the demos used for testing fork the Safari team's own showcase from the WebKit blog: a field of stars scattered at random and fading independently, a screen with a 100x100 grid painted in random colors, a roulette wheel built by Tim Nguyen, and three squares by Chris Coyier.

In the roulette demo, the minimum, maximum, and step use different units, as in random(2turn, 10turn, 20deg). The spec only requires the values to resolve to the same data type, which lets turn and deg mix.

Here is how it works. If a browser supports random() natively, the polyfill does nothing and steps aside. If not, it briefly hides randomized elements to prevent flicker, then scans the computed style for every property starting with --random.

The key is that custom property syntax is extremely permissive. Expressions the CSS parser can't interpret still survive as strings that JavaScript can read and handle. Browsers will resolve a var() substitution even when the surrounding value looks unrecognizable.

The random calculation itself wasn't written from scratch. He found @csstools/css-calc, an MIT-licensed library buried inside a PostCSS plugin. It has no dependencies, isn't tied to PostCSS, and recent commits have brought it up to the latest random() spec.

Values didn't scatter evenly at first. Without a specified base, the stars clumped together oddly. The author wrote that when users don't supply a base, he patched it by inserting a fixed random value.

The coverage is narrower than the native feature. The spec lets random() be used inside any property value, like calc(), but the polyfill requires an intermediate variable. In exchange, the code stays compatible with the native implementation. Once support is universal, removing it takes just one line of script.

There's a bonus too. He mimics random-item(), which no browser has implemented yet, in Chromium. It works by drawing an index with random(), then picking a value from a list using the CSS custom function --item and inline conditionals.

Meta pushed an update to the Quest 3 that significantly raised the refresh rate ceiling: up to 240Hz, or 207Hz at the headset's full resolution. Whether this extra headroom gets put to real use remains to be seen.
X user 'Luna' spotted it first. Horizon OS 2.7 added Extended Refresh Rates, opening up to 207Hz for regular users and up to 240Hz in developer mode.
Only the Quest 3 is affected. The Quest 3S and Quest 2 are not included. The Quest 3S uses a different panel and caps out at 120Hz.

240Hz comes with conditions. It requires developer mode and display scaling, which first lowers the resolution of the image sent to the panel and then upscales it. At full resolution, the ceiling is 207Hz.

blocks.cap: Image credit: Meta

blocks.x: A higher number doesn't mean the content follows. Native apps are mostly not built to target such high frame rates. 120Hz has been possible ever since the Quest 2 got experimental refresh rate support in April 2021, but apps that use that headroom remain rare even now.

The tools that used to stretch frames aren't pulling their weight right now either. Application Spacewarp, which doubles FPS with synthesized frames, doesn't mesh well with the Quest 3's SoC at high frame rates. Extrapolating past 120 FPS is already demanding, let alone 207 FPS.

PC VR is already moving. Virtual Desktop developer Guy Godin said on X that he added 144 FPS support to his app, which is used to stream a computer screen or run high-end PC VR games wirelessly. He added that the video decoder struggles past 144 FPS, so going higher looks unlikely.

Road to VR's Scott Hayden reads this update as a sign that the Quest 3 hardware always had unusually generous headroom. He wrote that it could also just be a common parting gift from companies trying to clear inventory near the end of a product's life.

Still, he doesn't think the Quest 3 is done. Valve's Steam Frame is about to announce its price and release date. As a headset that handles wireless PC VR streaming as well as downloading and running VR and flat games directly from Steam, it's already being compared to the Quest 3.

His guess goes like this: Meta hadn't unlocked the frame rate until now because it was focused on native Quest content, most of which can't even use 120Hz. With the Steam Frame closing in, it wants to show how far a $600 headset can go.
The Steam Frame will likely cost well over $1,000, and even its 144Hz only runs in an experimental mode. Getting people to set the two devices side by side is, by itself, a win for Meta.
Runway unveiled Solaris on August 31. It is the first model in a new line it calls the Interface World Model.
The starting point is a single question: what if the operating system generated apps and websites on the fly as you used them?

From early terminals through Linux and macOS, operating systems have decided what gets drawn on screen. Apps sit on top of that layer and stay fixed until someone pushes an update. Solaris draws that layer directly, compositing each frame the moment the user touches it.

The bottleneck Runway points to is the intermediate representation. Even a pixel-perfect mockup has to be translated into code before it moves. During that translation, only predefined behaviors survive, and visual density gets cut down too.
Solaris handles rendering and interaction in a single model. With no conversion step, there is no loss, and the entire frame becomes the interface.

blocks.cap: The result of reconstructing a web page from a single screenshot. The original is on the left; reconstructions by GPT-4o, Gemini 2.5 Pro, and Fable 5 are on the right.

blocks.x: The translation loss was measured numerically. Thirty interface types were handed to multimodal language models as a single screenshot each to reconstruct, and information preservation was measured with structural similarity (SSIM) and DINOv3 feature comparisons. Every model, including Claude Fable 5, lost information, and quality dropped consistently as visual complexity rose.

blocks.cap: Pairwise comparison results scored by 250 users.

blocks.x: It was also pitted directly against code-built interfaces. Starting from the same image and requesting the same manipulation, its output was placed side by side with Claude Opus 5's. 250 participants made about 7,500 judgments across 30 examples. Instruction-following split 61% to 24%, and when asked whether motion felt natural within the scene, it split 71% to 21%.

The architecture is a modified Gen-4.5 video generation model. Clicks and drags are accepted as conditioning for the next frame, just like text or images; frame generation was switched to be sequential, and the denoising stage was distilled down to a few steps. A language model decides how the scene should change, and the world model handles the drawing.

The remaining challenges are stated plainly. Text is the hardest part. Keeping legible characters stable in real time is still an open problem, and maintaining scene consistency over long sessions and working with accessibility tech like screen readers are also under study.
Solaris is still taking early access applications. Runway said it is preparing a public launch together with key partners.

Vercel released design.md. It's a file hosted at a single URL; no matter which tool an agent runs in, reading just this file lets it produce a page that looks like Vercel. Design engineer John Phamous laid out the process on August 31.

The starting point was an internal skill called product-design. Inside the repo, it lets an agent find and read the design system and product guidelines. The problem is outside the repo. Reports, proposals, and one-off pages get made in tools that can't read that file.

At first, they tried porting product-design straight into a public prompt. The sentences describing the visual language held up fine, but interpretation varied by model, and the same instructions produced completely different pages.

There were two reasons. Phrases like “keep the layout clean” mean practically nothing. The bigger issue was the missing context. Inside the repo, real components and deployed examples surround the skill, but in a public prompt there are only words.

So they dropped the port and rewrote it from scratch, bouncing off a fixed set of evaluation prompts the whole time. Seven of them, pulled from real work: a usage and performance report, a renewal proposal, a benchmark report, an interactive planning page, a build-versus-buy brief, and a presentation deck.

blocks.cap: Same prompt, data, model, and viewport, with design.md left out on one side and included on the other.

blocks.x: The first experiment was the renewal proposal. Run without design.md, it produced a generic SaaS dashboard. The version fed the file put the renewal recommendation up front and gathered the commercial case into a single grid. More than style shifted — structure and hierarchy did too.
The finished system has three layers: design.md holding judgment calls, a public stylesheet defining classes and tokens, and an evaluation loop that turns feedback into rules and automated checks.

blocks.cap: A piece of design.md. Naming a recurring 'generated' tell makes it easy to avoid.

blocks.x: The stylesheet was kept separate because the agent kept inventing its own typography and spacing. Header, table, stat-strip, and chart styles were bundled into CSS, posted at a public URL, with only the class names written into design.md.

One round means regenerating all seven scenarios from scratch with the current file, run on both Claude Opus 4.8 and Codex with GPT-5.5. Reviewer feedback was pushed down to whichever layer could enforce it most narrowly: judgment calls as prose, mechanics as stylesheet, anything a machine could check as a code check.

blocks.cap: A case where a table couldn't use its remaining width. Before and after pinning down a rule and a check.

blocks.x: Making the file took more than 200 generations. At the end, three desktop scenarios were generated with Codex with GPT-5.5, both with and without the file. Running automated checks on the six pages found 39 known failures versus 91 — 57% fewer.

Vercel added caveats too. The checks only catch failures it has already seen, six pages is too small a sample to argue about quality, and every page, with or without the file, still had flaws that would block a launch. Still, failures that were named and pinned down as rules tended not to reappear.

Keeping the file current comes down to real use. Calling @design-agent in Slack builds a page with the current design.md and returns a screenshot and a deployment URL. Recurring complaints get pulled out of the feedback that piles up each week, and people decide what to fix.
A report says Google is testing a 'Listening area' mode for Google Live Translate on Android XR. It could become a flagship feature of the upcoming smart glasses lineup.

Real-time translation is not a surprise, since Google has consistently said it would build the feature into Android XR. The company has also promised translated speech that keeps the speaker's tone and pitch, plus text translation for things like menus and signs, all on smart glasses.

Android Authority dug into version 10.32.66 of the Google Translate app and found the listening mode split into two. 'Front only' translates only the person directly in front of the wearer, suited to one-on-one conversation, while 'Surrounding area' uses the glasses' full microphone array to translate speech from everyone nearby.

Since this was found in the apk code, it is too early to guarantee an actual launch. Still, it fits Google's push to expand Android XR ahead of the smart glasses. Frames from Gentle Monster and Warby Parker are set to arrive first this fall, and frames from Kering, the parent company of Gucci, are reportedly also in the works.

Meta's smart glasses also include real-time translation, but Meta's version is closer to 'Front only.' Translated speech plays to the wearer through open-ear speakers, while the other person reads translated captions on the wearer's smartphone screen. Google, which leads in real-time translation, is expected to pack in as much functionality as possible here.

A few years ago, as AI tools began flooding in, Figma decided to track the fallout, from how people work to product strategy. The multi-year study, started in 2024, ran surveys each year, built an index, and gathered the stories behind the numbers through interviews. Thousands of data points and hundreds of transcripts were too much for people to handle by hand, so researcher Shane Johnston and his team built their own AI tools to run the research.

The first thing they built was a sentiment index. Like the University of Michigan's Consumer Sentiment Index, it captures how people feel rather than measuring the actual economy. The survey asks about what happened in the past 12 months alongside what people expect to change in the next 12 months. Comparing the two shows whether AI is catching up to expectations, exceeding them, or falling short. Answers range from 0 (no impact) to 100 (complete transformation). Around 50 means AI has become part of the work, and closer to 100 means the day-to-day has changed fundamentally.

The questions are organized around six axes — organizational goals, personal productivity, collaboration, projects, products and tools — and the same questions have been used for three years running. In 2026, all six axes came in more than 10 points above last year's projections. Collaboration nearly doubled, from 32 to 58, while personal productivity, projects and products climbed from the 40s into the high 60s and 70s.

blocks.cap: The Figma AI Impact Index shows respondents expect AI's influence to keep growing.

blocks.x: The index only shows what changed and by how much. This year, the team decided to hear directly from the people who lived through that change and added an AI interview tool. An AI moderator asked real-time follow-up questions and steered the conversation based on context, running 639 sessions. That produced 639 transcripts, 2 million words, 40,701 codes, 11,846 themes, and 553 themes that recurred across participants.

Off-the-shelf analysis tools do not show their inner workings. Without visibility into the interpretation process, there is no way to verify it. So the team rebuilt thematic analysis — reading every transcript, coding each statement, and grouping statements into larger themes — so each step could be inspected. Selecting the theme “AI sped up iteration but raised quality concerns” brings up the 47 participants who mentioned it, with a path to each person's statement and the original transcript.

blocks.cap: The thematic analysis pipeline found and named themes from the interview transcripts.

blocks.x: It was not just about speed. When people manually review hundreds of transcripts by hand, fatigue builds and interpretation drifts, making it easy to code the 50th interview differently from the first. The tool applied the same standard every time. Still, the team could not hand everything over wholesale, so they specified exactly which methods to use and how to handle conflicting themes. MIT economist David Autor called this re-intermediation of expertise: AI does not remove expert judgment, it makes that judgment repeatable.

Once the tool solved one problem, another appeared. Tens of thousands of data points were scattered across laptops and text files, hard for anyone but the researchers to dig through, yet the report also had writers, marketers and analysts attached to it. So the team built an internal dashboard pulling together three years of survey results, interview analysis, and trends by role and region. They turned the raw-data analysis into a self-contained HTML document, went back and forth a few times with the Figma MCP server, and deployed it with Payload CMS, which also handled version control and access permissions.

blocks.cap: This dashboard lets anyone on the team open the data directly.

blocks.x: Instead of scattered emails and slides painting different pictures, everyone looked at the same material. This year's index came in at 62 out of 100, nearly double 2024's score. The change was already visible before the analysis was even finished; the index just put a number on it.

Coding agents are changing how development works, but they still only perform as well as the context they're given. In its Workflow Lab series, Figma shared a sequence that moves between canvas and code while preserving design intent. The tools involved are Figma Design and FigJam, along with the Figma MCP server, Code Connect, use_figma, generate_diagram, search_design_system and get_variable_defs.

The setting is Radicle, a fictional STEM learning app. Work that used to take weeks now takes days, sometimes hours, but the speed hasn't translated into results, because AI-generated code keeps drifting from the design spec. On this task, an inbox redesign, handing over just a screenshot and a dev ticket led to misaligned icons, uneven modal spacing, and a toast missing its failure state. It's a batch-processing flow spanning three screens: toolbar, modal and toast.

blocks.cap: Radicle's new inbox toolbar, supporting select all, mark as unread, and delete.

blocks.x: The developer doesn't start with code. They write up the screens, states and transitions, then hand the agent the PRD along with the existing component code. Then they use generate_diagram to create an editable diagram in FigJam. Select all checks every message. Delete triggers a confirmation modal, and undo on the toast rolls the dashboard back to its previous state. The designer and the design system lead left comments directly on the diagram instead of in a Slack thread.

blocks.cap: Passing along the FigJam diagram together with the library lets the agent find the components and variables to use.

blocks.x: Once approval is done, the diagram is handed to the agent through the Figma MCP server. With only a screenshot, the developer would have had to go ask whether a 12 px gap matched a token, or whether that button was already a secondary one in the repo. Now the answer is in the file. Code Connect fills in how each component was built. Once the design system lead links the library to the GitHub repository and writes template files for the button and modal, the agent starts from an existing implementation instead of writing new code.

Only the batch-select state was newly created, so Code Connect couldn't map it. The developer searched the team library with search_design_system and found a similar component from a feature shipped months earlier. The agent found it in the codebase and adapted it to fit this flow.

While the modal was being built, the design changed. The brand color got darker and the button corner radius changed. Instead of fixing it by hand, the developer called get_variable_defs to pull the variables the modal used, and the agent cross-checked them against the code tokens and immediately caught two mismatches.

That left the toast. It was created during the build, existed only in code, and had no failure state. Using use_figma to bring the toast onto the canvas as an editable layer, the designer added a retry action, and after the design system lead shipped the new component, it was linked to the code with Code Connect. From there, it went like any other release: most of the pull request's diff was feature logic. The engineer reviewed the code, and the designer looked at the preview build. The time once spent reworking AI-generated code shifted into time spent polishing the user experience.

This is an episode of The Unlock from the Adobe Creative Cloud channel. It captures a working graphic designer's approach to product mockups in 1 minute 34 seconds. Badal Patel, who founded the studio Super Spicy, uses Adobe Firefly together with Photoshop and Illustrator.

The subject is the nail polish brand Static. In the video, Patel says she created the brand herself to tell the story of being a new mom. She opens by comparing her work to a single bite that delivers sweet, salty, and funky flavors all at once.

The starting point was a single photo. She uploaded the photo to Adobe Firefly and started adjusting prompts, because she wanted to see quickly how the brand would come to life. Firefly builds the bottle that's in her head.

The prompt included the idea that it might be more interesting if the bottle looked like it was about to topple over. Firefly produced exactly that composition, and made it look like it had actually been shot. Patel decided to carry that playfulness over into geometric shapes to create the nail polish bottle's packaging.

Next comes Adobe Photoshop. She reworked everything by hand until she was satisfied. Then she added the logo made in Adobe Illustrator, plus grain and a subtle drop shadow, to finish it off so it looked like a real object.

She says this let her deliver a strong visual punch when showing mockups to clients and pitching ideas. Adobe presents this video as an example of communicating with clients while conveying creative intent clearly and precisely.
To human eyes, the Digital Camouflage shirt is an abstract pattern of green, pink, and orange shapes jumbled together. To a robot, it hides the person wearing it.

German designer Simon Weckert made it. After surveillance cameras were installed in Berlin earlier this year, he built this button-up shirt to confuse AI surveillance systems. It sits within a broader movement of adversarial clothing design that uses complex patterns to disrupt facial and object recognition.

blocks.cap: The Digital Camouflage shirt (Image: Simon Weckert)

blocks.x: “Object detection systems don't 'see' the way we do,” Weckert told Fast Company. “They scan images for statistical patterns—combinations of contours, textures, and colors that have been trained to be bundled with the category 'person.'”
The pattern was mathematically optimized to send the wrong signal to that neural network. Selling for about $88, the shirt has to do double duty: throw off AI while still being wearable.

blocks.cap: The pattern sits between human taste and algorithmic demands (Image: Simon Weckert)

blocks.x: “An adversarial pattern straight out of optimization works, but it's visually chaotic. It's an image purely for machines.” The final pattern landed right in the middle of algorithmic demands and human taste, and Weckert says that ambiguity matters conceptually. “It's a garment that speaks to two kinds of viewers at once. Each sees something completely different.”

It's closer to raising the question of how trustworthy a technology can be if a single piece of fabric can unravel it.

AI image systems produce a plausible-looking room in seconds. But a concept image is neither a construction drawing nor a shopping list. The hard work begins after generation: translating pixels into a plan that respects dimensions, circulation, light, fixtures, budget, and the things already in the house. This workflow treats the AI concept as a visual hypothesis and tests its assumptions before any money goes out the door. With a measured sketch, a spreadsheet, and a consistent review sequence, most early decisions can be handled without full CAD.

blocks.cap: A Measurement-First Workflow for Evaluating AI Interior Concepts

blocks.x: Start by setting the input brief. Note the room type, the main activities, how many people use it regularly, items that must stay, and the budget range. Add constraints a photo can't reveal: lease terms, pets, children, accessibility, and electrical fixtures to be installed. The key move is separating requirements from preferences. “Keep an 850mm clear path from the door to the window” is a requirement; “a warm neutral palette” is a preference. Violate a requirement and the concept is disqualified; a preference can simply be adjusted.

Next comes a trustworthy measurement model. Measure wall lengths, ceiling height, doors, windows, radiators, outlets, switches, and built-in furniture. Wide-angle lenses distort distance and size, so photos alone won't give you a reliable scale. Set one corner as (0, 0) and record fixed elements as intervals along each wall—for example, a window on the north wall starting 920mm from the west corner with a width of 1,450mm. Measure critical dimensions twice.

At the generation stage, produce alternatives rather than a single answer. Hold geometry and must-have items fixed, and change only one thing at a time—layout, lighting emphasis, material palette, or storage strategy. If every variable changes at once between images, there's no way to tell what actually improved the room. Attach a prompt version and a short hypothesis to each result, and keep rejected concepts as evidence of recurring failure patterns.

A scale audit comes next. For each concept, find at least three reference objects whose rough size you already know—a standard door, a sofa you're keeping. Look for the common errors of image generation: an impossible chair depth, an oversized pendant light. Transfer candidate furniture to the measured sketch using manufacturer dimensions or a conservative estimate. If a must-have item only fits by cutting into minimum clearances or blocking a door swing, the concept is disqualified.

Look at circulation as a graph: set entrances, seating, storage, work surfaces, and windows as nodes, and connect the paths between them. Measure the effective width at the narrowest point, not the average. A dining table that only works if every chair is pushed in isn't a solid plan. Audit lighting separately by time and task—generated images draw light that ignores orientation and time of day. A simple table with activities as rows and morning, afternoon, and evening as columns will catch most obvious conflicts.

Tie storage to an inventory list, not to the image—include cables, chargers, cleaning tools, paperwork, and AV equipment. Habits matter as much as capacity: if the household drops keys and bags at the entryway, make space right there instead of in a distant cabinet. Then map out dependencies. Electrical work, wall repair, painting, flooring, built-ins, and movable furniture have a sequence. For each task, note who's responsible, the estimate, prerequisites, and the cost of reversing it.

The last step is a physical check. Mark furniture placement and circulation on the floor with masking tape, and build cardboard mockups of large, tall items to live with for a few days. Screen colors can't be trusted for paint or wood, so view samples in the actual room. The final output isn't a picture—it's a bundle of decisions backed by evidence, dimensions, and a construction sequence.

From the AI art controversy around Spider-Man: Brand New Day to Masters of the Universe, those who used AI have had one main line of defense: it was just concept art. The AI-generated images, they say, never made it into the final film.

But concept art is still art. It ends up in art books and behind-the-scenes footage, where fans pore over it for years. If a film becomes iconic enough, that artwork becomes a historical artifact. A recent Disney art auction showed, once again, just how much artistic—and financial—value that kind of work can hold.

blocks.cap: Original art for Snow White by Gustaf Tenggren (Image: Disney / Heritage Auctions)

blocks.x: Just days after marveling at the sheer number of characters Disney crammed into this year's D23 poster design, a batch of rare original art and posters went up for auction, a reminder of the animation studio's deep legacy. The Disney art auction Heritage Auctions held last weekend brought in $3.43 million across 1,346 lots, spanning everything from the Golden Age through the Disney Renaissance to films from the 2000s.

The most notable pieces were original artworks Gustaf Tenggren drew for Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs. A scene of Snow White listening to the Prince sing “One Song” sold for $85,400. A panoramic drawing of six of the seven dwarfs returning home went for $41,480, and a drawing of the Prince on horseback sold for $36,600.

blocks.cap: A panoramic drawing of six dwarfs returning home, $41,480 (Image: Disney / Heritage Auctions)

blocks.x: The top sales also included two pieces by Mary Blair. A colorful concept painting of the Japan section of It's a Small World sold for $31,720, and an original concept-and-color-key piece depicting Alice, the Mad Hatter, and the White Rabbit at the tea party in Alice in Wonderland went for $29,280.

blocks.cap: Original concept-and-color-key artwork from Alice in Wonderland (Image: Disney / Heritage Auctions)

blocks.x: The Joe Ranft family archive yielded storyboards and concept art from Toy Story, A Bug's Life, Monsters, Inc, and Cars.

blocks.cap: A Toy Story storyboard hand-colored by Joe Ranft (Image: Disney / Heritage Auctions)

blocks.x: “This response speaks to the global affection for Disney and to a growing recognition of animation art as a significant art form,” said Jim Lentz, Heritage's Vice President of Animation Art and Anime Art.
Using AI for concept art speeds things up. But will anyone say the same thing, 50 years from now, about an AI-generated Spider-Man drawing?
