Viewed from outside, 'AI CAD' can easily look like generative 3D modeling with marketing stacked on top: you enter a prompt and a mesh comes out, the same category as image generation, just with objects as the target. If you're actually making things to manufacture, or evaluating tools for that, this assumption is wrong.

A mesh is a pile of triangles. There's no concept of "this hole is 8mm because an M8 bolt has to go through it" or "this wall is 2mm because that's the minimum thickness for this material." There are only vertices, edges and faces frozen at their current positions. Most AI 3D tools trained on the same pipeline as image generation output meshes. That's great for games, VFX and visualization, but not for manufacturing.

A parametric model is different starting from the data structure itself. It's a sequence of features—extrudes, fillets, holes with a set diameter and depth—and each feature is defined by relationships and dimensions rather than fixed triangle coordinates. Change a diameter parameter and the geometry beneath it changes all at once. This is also the structure that professional CAD tools like SolidWorks, Fusion 360 and Onshape work with internally, and STEP files, tolerance stacks, GD&T and CAM toolpaths all depend on it. None of that works on top of a mesh.

So the real question to ask an 'AI CAD' tool isn't whether it can make a 3D shape from text. It's what data structure sits on the other side of that generation. The answer decides whether you got something to look at or something to make.

Pulling a mesh out of a prompt is a relatively easy ML problem, because it's close to the image and video generation paradigm that most generative 3D research rides on. Producing a valid parametric feature tree is different and harder. It has to be a consistent sequence of manufacturable operations, not just a plausible-looking surface, and if even one step is geometrically out of line with the one before it, the whole tree collapses.

The author's own project, CadXStudio, is said to have taken this problem on directly rather than working around it. The output isn't a mesh dressed up to look like CAD, but a B-Rep model built from parametric features, exported as STEP, with STL and OBJ also produced for printing and visualization. That's why dimensions or fillet radii can be fixed without rebuilding from scratch, and why machinists and CAM tools can take the STEP file as is. It's also why faces that meet and holes that align can reference each other and bind into an assembly.

The fastest way to judge a tool is to check what happens after generation. When you select a face, can you see a dimension you can edit? When you export to STEP and open it in 'real' CAD, does it quietly turn into a dumb solid? Does changing one parameter bring the dependent geometry along with it, or does 'editing' ultimately mean writing another prompt? These questions are what separate a rendering engine from a design engine. One gives you something to look at; the other gives you something to make.

No one buys a design-to-code tool because it makes hero sections look pretty. A designer uploads a messy SaaS dashboard to Figma, the team has to receive it in React and Next.js by Friday, and they just don't want to spend the weekend untangling div soup.

So the test case for this benchmark is a single screen from an old, practical dashboard: nested auto layouts, haphazard naming, a dated sidebar and top nav, dense tables, forms with error states, and a few modals and popovers. The same Figma export and the same component rules were fed identically into five tools.

The scoring criteria are accessibility (number of axe-core violations and Lighthouse score), the ratio of semantic tags, the size of the production bundle and dependency count, the cost of making edits, and finally, visual fidelity. Edit cost was measured by actually implementing three requests—persisting sidebar collapse state, a checkbox column with a bulk-action bar for the table, and inline validation messages for the form—and counting the files touched and the lines of code added or removed.

Scores run from 1 to 10. The Dev Mode baseline scored 9 on accessibility, semantics, bundle and editability, with 8 on fidelity—slowest to start, fastest to maintain. The token-aware exporter scored 7, 7, 8, 7, 7; the component-mapping AI tool scored 6, 6, 6, 6, 8. The screenshot-based generator scored 9 on fidelity but only 3 on accessibility and semantics, and 2 on editability. The full-stack platform scored 5, 5, 4, 5, 7, with the heaviest bundle of all.

The screenshot tool's failure showed up clearly on the sidebar-collapse request. It looked fine on the surface, but it wasn't a component with a layout contract—just a pile of stacked containers. By contrast, the tools that used deterministic input, like tokens and components, came out ahead on ease of editing. The generator that built the dashboard table as a div grid instead of a table with th scope lost points on accessibility immediately.

The recommendation depends on the team. For a startup that needs to ship v1 fast, the author says to use the screenshot tool only for prototyping and be prepared to rewrite the UI layer later. For a company where accessibility and compliance are on the line, this path is better not treated as the main route. Teams with a solid design system should invest in a token pipeline; development-led teams that already have a component library should invest in a tool that maps to that library. If you can't reproduce the output, that's not a benchmark—it's content marketing.

blocks.cap: One spec, four renderers. The whole argument is in this single image.

blocks.x: Connection was the easy part. The plumbing for MCP servers is mostly settled, essentially HTTP dressed up for the AI era. What isn't settled is what the client does when an agent needs to put a date picker on screen: which components exist, who owns the rendering, and what it looks like once it's there.

There are four approaches, and every product worth caring about falls into one of them. No one has published a comparison chart, so sorting out which client belongs where took four specs, one protocol proposal, and one Google engineering blog post. Even the names they use for things differ.

Google is trying to build that standard with A2UI, short for agent-to-UI. Released in December 2025, the approach is declarative: an agent sends JSON naming components that already exist in the client's catalog, and the client renders it with its own code. Neither markup nor styling crosses the line. 1.0 is still a release candidate and resembles HTML constructs from 1999. Even so, it's the only proposal not owned by a single vendor.

blocks.cap: The approaches Claude and ChatGPT support look alike, but each is actually an IFRAME going into its own client.

blocks.x: Google Gemini Enterprise, Opal, and OpenClaw Canvas render standard A2UI components without carrying a separate renderer. On the other side is sandboxed HTML. OpenAI's ChatGPT renders app UIs with the Apps SDK, and Anthropic's Claude does it with Artifacts and MCP Apps, which carries its own renderer. Expressiveness is large, control is hard, and wherever it lands, it remains a web object.

There's also the non-A2UI camp. Microsoft Teams and Outlook render Adaptive Cards through seven renderer SDKs, and Slack renders Block Kit. Same approach, just a single owner. Consumer Gemini rebuilds its UI fresh with every prompt, and xAI's Grok has no surface at all.

blocks.cap: Surfaces × platforms. The same date picker gets specified and built over and over.

blocks.x: The cost shows up as a tax, not a licensing fee. Every added surface increases what the design system has to support, and the platforms multiply it further. Add web, iOS, and Android to ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Copilot inside Teams and Outlook, and Slack. Ten surfaces across three platforms isn't a ten-item problem — it's building the same date picker once in Block Kit JSON, again as an Adaptive Card, and again in whatever format ChatGPT wants.

The browser wars are the precedent. Netscape and Microsoft hurled tags at each other in the late 1990s, and caught between document.layers and document.all, most sites carried browser-detection code up top and two full sets of layout underneath. When Internet Explorer 6 won, the web stalled for five years. Agentic UI is the old browser war in new clothes, and this time the names are ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Copilot, and Slack.

Author Patrick Neeman wrote that there are four things to do first. Draw a matrix with surfaces and platforms as axes and write an owner in every cell. Write a catalog, not screens. Specify, with versions, the roughly twelve components agents need to get work done — tables, forms, date pickers, confirmations, states, errors, empty states — including their states and constraints, so the work survives whichever format wins. Read the Adaptive Cards schema first. Test your first agent form not on a desktop but on a mid-range Android device with TalkBack turned on.

The Coinbase Design System (CDS) team supports the mobile and web products of America's largest cryptocurrency exchange, for both individual and institutional users. The team has grown the system around quality, consistency, and accessibility — but what should change when the primary user shifts from engineers to agents? Tech lead Erich Kuerschner found his answer in the Figma MCP server, Code Connect, and CDS's agent skills. Running his own evaluation, he found Code Connect cut costs by an average of 22.5% and work time by about 22%.

blocks.cap: An overview of the Coinbase Design System's components

blocks.x: He says his tests showed that Code Connect reduces the number of tokens agents need when translating Figma designs into code. The context Code Connect provides also makes code quality noticeably better, he says.

The CDS team already had several skills that taught agents the design system's best practices: choosing the right component, avoiding deprecated components and patterns, and using CDS design tokens. On top of that, they built an internal prototyping playground. But both were geared toward writing code from scratch, leaving a gap in the common task of turning Figma designs into product-grade CDS code. Product engineers said the process was slow, inaccurate, and unpredictable, making it hard to fit into daily work.

blocks.cap: The personal information input form used for testing

blocks.x: Code Connect was the lever, but the mapping had stalled before the Figma MCP server launched. What remained was outdated, and many new components didn't even have templates. Hundreds of components across mobile and web needed attention. Erich Kuerschner built an agentic workflow in Claude Code to scan the Figma component list in parallel, with the figma-code-connect skill writing the templates. In four hours, the entire design system had moved over to the new Code Connect format.

The evaluation ran three times on an empty codebase, using the same design, the same prompt, and the same model (Sonnet 4.6). Each run started fresh, and the effect of prompt caching was controlled for. The prompt was deliberately vague — a single line reading "Implement this design from Figma." The header included a trap: a CDS Stepper with dozens of properties. Agents inventing names for illustrations and icons had also been a long-standing headache, and that problem disappeared overnight once Code Connect was fully attached.

blocks.cap: Average token use down 11.5%, implementation time down 22.3%, cost down 22.5%

blocks.x: All three runs finished the same work more cheaply and faster. The evaluation also drew a clear line between what the two tools do. The CDS agent skills shape how an agent implements a solution, while Code Connect hands over the best possible context upfront when starting from a design. Getting component context first meant fewer tokens spent searching and guessing.

With each model generation, agents use CDS well even without the skills. Erich Kuerschner sees the evaluation as preparation for a time when skills become unnecessary. The quality of context still matters then. He said he doesn't want to be left without Code Connect in that future, because he's already seen what happens when an agent interprets a design however it likes.

blocks.cap: The accessible tetrad color harmony Perplexity suggested, applied to a data visualization example.

blocks.x: In this piece, author Theresa-Marie Rhyne examines how Perplexity suggests tetrad color harmonies that pass color-blindness tests. Perplexity is a text-based generative AI. She had previously looked at recommendations from DeepSeek, ChatGPT, Claude, Copilot, and Gemini in the same way.

At first, Perplexity steered its answer narrowly toward color blindness and failed to produce a proper tetrad. Only after revising the prompt and asking again did it return a tetrad close to the target. The author points out the problems that surfaced along the way.

The main discussion starts with an overview of tetrad color harmony, color blindness, and text-based generative AI. Color harmony is the practice of choosing colors from a color wheel that work well together when composing an image. Similar to a concept in music, combinations on a color wheel become a shared baseline for how colors relate to one another. The idea of the color wheel traces back to Isaac Newton, who closed a linear color spectrum into a circle in the early 1700s, and painters and color scientists later extended it into color harmony.
The rest of the piece is available only to paid members, so this translation covers only the publicly available opening section.
Dassault Systèmes introduced a Blue Token subscription to charge for AI usage across the 3DExperience platform.

A few weeks ago, we reported that Dassault Systèmes' virtual companions Aura, Leo, and Marie had all gone live on 3DExperience. We then spoke with Solidworks CEO Manish Kumar about the rollout and what it means for users.

There's one important update. The July 23 launch announcement made no mention that a new billing system was rolling out alongside the virtual companions. Kumar said people may not have noticed that tokens started shipping with it too.

It was expected. Back in February, Kumar said he would introduce a consumption-based license that bundled units of knowledge, know-how, and work into “something easy to understand.” That something is the Blue Token. It's hard to find a simpler name than a primary color.

Every query to Aura, Leo, or Marie costs Blue Tokens — simple requests cost less, complex ones cost more. Right now, a pack of 25,000 sells for $1,250 a year, and tokens expire at year's end. Kumar said Solidworks users get 2,000 free per license.
Dassault Systèmes' FAQ says a single pack of 25,000 Blue Tokens can cover thousands of quick insights, dozens of complex generative builds, or a mix of both.

Let's go a bit deeper. Each companion has areas Dassault Systèmes calls competencies, and competencies are made up of skills. The one closest to Solidworks users is Leo, an engineer-type companion with mechanical design competency. According to Kumar, Leo's most popular skill so far has been assembly performance analysis, which optimizes assemblies.

blocks.cap: Leo helps with assembly performance in Solidworks. (Image: Dassault Systèmes)

blocks.x: Next is model insights, a feature that lets users ask natural-language questions about their own models — things like which parts in this assembly are made of aluminum, or what the surface area of this part is. Internally it's called ChatWorks, and Kumar said it's very simple yet very powerful. Asked how much it costs to count aluminum parts, he said about 5 to 10 cents — one or two Blue Tokens.

The third skill, drawing generation, is being used more and more. It automatically produces 2D drawings from 3D models. Kumar said they're developing it toward training on user data so drawings come out using weights customized for that specific customer.

Kumar didn't offer an estimate for the cost of generated drawings, saying it varies widely. He noted only that costs rise with model complexity, and that custom-trained inference is more expensive than using default weights.

Whether it's Blue Tokens, Red Credits, or Green Funbucks, consumption-based licensing has become the default for AI tools. It's hard to blame Dassault Systèmes for following the trend. Still, it doesn't sit easily. Having covered the shift from perpetual CAD seats to subscriptions for a long time, it's hard to shake the feeling that the water is heating up again the same way it did back then — a transition that worked for vendors and left a residue of resentment among users.
It's 4:52 p.m. on a Friday, and a message goes up in the bug channel: “The dashboard won't load.” The only attachment is a single screenshot of a spinner.

blocks.cap: Agent-Native Clips captures a recording together with browser diagnostics

blocks.x: Ask for a video, and ten minutes later a link arrives: someone opening the project, waiting, getting an error banner. It proves the bug is real, but it says nothing about why it happened.

That's when the ritual begins: open the app, log in with that account, open dev tools, check the console, switch to the network tab, refresh, find the failed request, and copy the status code. The recording only captured the symptom, and the evidence stayed trapped inside a browser you can't get into.

Agent-Native Clips fills that gap. It's a free, open-source screen recorder that, while recording, also collects console output, failed network requests, HTTP status codes, and the context before and after the moment something broke. Record once, and the video goes to whoever needs to watch it while the diagnostic data goes to whoever needs to fix it.

On the surface, it behaves just like any other async recording tool: capture the browser, add mic and camera, save, share a link. The difference is what the clip carries with it. Record with the Chrome extension, and browser-level diagnostics come attached.

What gets attached: console logs and errors, failed network requests, HTTP status codes, the timing and context around the failure, and structured metadata an AI coding agent can read. The app runs locally or on a free hosted version.

blocks.cap: The browser diagnostics collected alongside the recording

blocks.x: It's clear why a screen recording alone stalls the fix: finding out which endpoint failed, whether the response was a 401 or a 502, or whether the frontend got odd data still requires someone to open dev tools and dig from scratch. Reproducing a bug three times can even change the conditions along the way. With Clips, that loop shrinks to four steps: start recording, reproduce, stop, share.

Setup has two parts: the Clips app, which runs locally or in the cloud, and a Chrome extension that starts the recording and gathers diagnostics. It's better to pin the extension to the toolbar. No one digs through an extension menu the moment a bug hits.

In the demo, a network error appears the moment the app opens, and the browser logs several failed requests, including 502s and 401s. A 502 shows up when a gateway or proxy gets a bad response from an upstream service; a 401 shows up when a request lacks authentication.

A saved clip bundles that session's console messages and network errors together as JSON. It's not a format made for easy reading. It's not data meant for a human to scroll through, it's data meant for a tool to process.

That's why a clip reads two ways at once: a person watches the video, a machine tears into the data. You can hand it to an AI assistant and ask it to trace the request causing the 502 back through the code and propose a fix, or ask it to turn it into a GitHub issue with reproduction steps, expected behavior, actual behavior, and the browser errors.

It isn't only a developer's tool. A designer can upload a broken screen found during review without ever learning the network tab, and a PM can send along the exact sequence of events with technical evidence attached. The source is open on GitHub, so self-hosting is just a fork away.
ArtStation has rolled out stronger measures, saying it will protect artists' work from unauthorized AI training and also keep generated images from flooding the platform.

Starting today, the NoAI setting is turned on for every new project uploaded. The tag is also applied retroactively to projects and profiles that were already up. There's no need to go through an old portfolio piece by piece.

The NoAI tag marks a piece of work as off-limits for AI training. Anyone who wants to allow training can just turn the setting off. The structure has flipped: protection used to require a request, and now protection is the default that you opt out of if you want.

blocks.cap: The NoAI setting applies to both new uploads and existing projects

blocks.x: Crawler blocking is done in partnership with Cloudflare. It works by identifying known AI crawlers and automated scraping tools and stopping them before they can access content in bulk. The company acknowledges there's no way to make public images completely unscrapable. Still, it says the goal is to make unauthorized access harder and to keep adjusting its defenses as the technology changes.

In its announcement, ArtStation wrote that the community's demand was clear and that it agrees with it. The statement closed with the line: “There's no reason artists should have to ask first to protect their own work.”
Indexing by ordinary search engines stays open. Recruiters, studios, and potential clients can still find portfolios just as they do now.

The terms of service were updated as well. Under the current AI policy, ownership of the work stays with the artist, and ArtStation does not sell or license that work to AI companies. There are also no agreements that permit AI companies to collect the content.
The announcement didn't stop at the training issue. The company itself admitted that its current CreatedWithAI label and filters haven't been enough to hold back the flood of generated images.

blocks.cap: It also addressed generated images overwhelming the discovery system

blocks.x: Artists have long argued that as generated work piles up, original work becomes harder to find and portfolios become harder to evaluate. The company says it is improving its discovery tools and adding more controls, but hasn't yet explained how or when those will arrive.

This move comes right after Kitbash acquired ArtStation and Sketchfab. Kitbash is the company behind Kitbash3D and Greyscalegorilla. The deal, announced in August, split both platforms off from Epic Games, while existing portfolios, libraries, subscriptions, marketplaces, and workflows stayed in place.

That doesn't mean AI-made images are banned. Work made with AI tools can still be posted, as long as you own it or have permission to post it. If a product sold on the marketplace includes generative AI output, it needs the CreatedWithAI tag.

For artists who have been demanding that generated work be removed entirely, this line may still fall short. Even so, turning on NoAI for existing uploads too is a sign that ArtStation's default has actually shifted.
Cursor Cloud Agents can now run inside Vercel Sandbox instead of on machines operated by Cursor.

blocks.cap: Cursor Cloud Agents running in Vercel Sandbox

blocks.x: Cursor still manages the agent harness and the inference loop itself. Its Self-Hosted Machines API only pulls in the execution environment from outside: you supply the place where repositories get cloned, files get edited, and commands and tests get run. This feature is available only on the Cursor Enterprise plan.

Vercel Sandbox creates that place by spinning up an isolated Firecracker microVM for every single agent request. Vercel Functions and Vercel Workflow handle the control plane: picking up pending requests, spinning up workers, watching sessions, and cleaning up on their own.

This setup delivers four things: a worker pool that can scale down to zero without any long-lived virtual machines, a dedicated sandbox attached to each request, durable retries when a worker or session dies, and user-scoped credentials that live only briefly, inside the sandbox.
Vercel also published a step-by-step guide for deploying the reference implementation to your own account, along with Sandbox documentation.
Manchester City's new kit is the first professional football kit designed by fans using AI, and it's actually worn on the pitch.

blocks.cap: Manchester City's new fan-designed third kit

blocks.x: This third kit, unveiled by the Premier League club, came out of Puma AI Creator, a generative AI tool built in-house by the German sportswear brand Puma.

Puma launched this generator in December 2024. Its engine is the AI co-creation platform Deepobjects, paired with text prompts and sliders for adjusting elements like the collar, colors, and badge placement. Last year, Ederson, Stefan Ortega, and Rico Lewis used AI to create a green goalkeeper kit with a goal-net pattern. The club then opened the tool to the public for the rest of its kits.

blocks.cap: A design concept made with Puma AI Creator

blocks.x: People in more than 200 countries created over 180,000 designs, drawing more than 1.7 million votes. The platform gave participants design credits and two entries, with more credits and entries available for rating other people's designs or holding a Puma NFT.

blocks.cap: The finalist designs narrowed down by vote

blocks.x: Among the ten finalists, the winner was a prompt by Elliott, a lifelong Man City supporter. He said he made it during his lunch break. Down the middle of a white jersey run two gradient blue vertical stripes, one sky blue and one navy. The front carries the club badge, the Puma logo, and the logo of sponsor Etihad Airways. The fabric is Puma's lightweight performance material, Ultraweave.

Unlike adversarial designs made to confuse AI systems, the winning design has no bizarre or dizzying patterns. A white kit with sky blue and navy vertical stripes is something the club has worn before, as it did in a Nike-made kit for the 2013-14 season.

blocks.cap: The winning design made into an actual kit

blocks.x: Even so, this kit marks a turning point in how professional sports is embracing AI. The club said it's the first case of a fan-designed, AI-made kit being worn on a football pitch. Comments on the club's own post included criticism calling it “AI slop” and saying it lacked originality.

blocks.cap: ArmorPaint, now an official release after eight years

blocks.x: The Armory development team has released ArmorPaint 1.0, an open source 3D texture painting program. It's the 'official' version, arriving eight years after entering early access in 2018.

This release rewrites the software in C. With the performance gain, it can paint much larger 3D assets in real time and stack more texture layers at higher resolution. New additions include basic sculpting and UV editing, skinned-character timeline playback, AI image upscaling, and a feature that turns photos into materials.

Downloads are open for Windows, Linux, and macOS, with Android and iOS as experimental builds. As of this writing, the product website carries no official release announcement, but the early-release-candidate label has disappeared from the download list.

ArmorPaint is a 3D painting tool for building PBR texture maps used in DCC software or game engines. It's often cited as a cheaper alternative to Adobe Substance 3D Painter. You paint directly onto a model's surface in a real-time path-traced viewport, and because it's GPU-based, high-end GPUs can paint up to 16K. It bakes AO, Cavity, Thickness, normal, material ID, and lightmaps, and exports to PNG, JPEG, and EXR at up to 32-bit color depth.

blocks.cap: 1.0 (blue bars) is faster than 0.9 (gray bars)

blocks.x: Code originally written in Haxe with the JavaScript engine V8 layered on top is now entirely C. No external libraries are needed either. GPU acceleration runs on Direct3D 12, Vulkan, Metal, and WebGPU, while ray tracing runs on Direct3D 12 on Windows, Vulkan on Linux and Android, and Metal on macOS and iOS. The codebase has shrunk enough that, in the development blog's own phrasing, it would fit on two old 1.4MB floppy disks. More importantly, it uses far less memory. You can open large models and paint high-resolution textures without changing your hardware.

blocks.cap: A new tile-sheet creation plugin for game artists

blocks.x: New features include a basic digital sculpting mode. Decimate, Subdivide, Smooth, and Bevel modifiers for working with imported geometry, plus a basic UV editor, are also included. Path and curve layers let you add stitching or geometric patterns, and the timeline tab plays back skinned mesh animation or lets you build simple tween animations. 'Neural Nodes' handle image upscaling, converting images to PBR textures, and text-to-image generation. All supported models are open source and run locally on a workstation or tablet.
The source code is free under the zlib license. Compiled binaries that support development cost $19 on itch.io; the iOS app is $17.99 and the Android app is $19.99.

The author opened GitHub last Tuesday and found the main deploy pipeline all red. Staging was completely dead. The cause: two frontend teams had edited the Tailwind config file at the same time. Team A had added spacing utilities for a marketing landing page; Team B added brand colors for a new product dashboard. While resolving the merge conflict by hand and force-pushing, half the core brand colors disappeared and the production deploy stopped.

This is what always happens when a single config file becomes a bottleneck. A developer copies hex codes and pixel values from Figma by hand and pastes them into a giant JavaScript object. Someone makes a typo. Someone deletes a bracket. The author decided to take the human out of this step. Figma is the source of truth for design decisions, Tailwind is the destination, and code is what connects the two.

The token file uses the W3C Design Token format, a standard JSON structure that specifies values and types explicitly, making it easy to predict. A TypeScript utility was attached to it. It skips meta keys starting with a dollar sign, recursively walks the token tree to produce flat keys like brand-primary, and then writes a tailwind.preset.js module to disk. The main Tailwind config now simply imports this preset.

A GitHub Action handles execution. The workflow only runs on pull requests where tokens.json has changed; it runs the conversion script and then commits the updated preset straight into the same pull request. When a designer changes a variable in Figma, a pull request opens with the new JSON, and the developer just reviews the code and hits merge.

The author added that maintaining a hand-built conversion script gets annoying once typography rules grow complex or dark-mode themes multiply. That's what led to building the Figma plugin Design System Sync. It exports variables and styles to GitHub or Bitbucket and automatically opens a pull request with a visual diff attached. The free tier gives you five exports a month.
This is a one-minute video Figma posted. It covers timestamped comments in Figma Motion, which tie a comment to a specific moment in the animation rather than the whole file.
Leaving one is simple. Pick [Comment] from the toolbar, then move the playhead to the point you want to mark. Click the animation while in that state, and the comment attaches to that moment.
The video has four segments: 00:00 introduction, 00:10 how to add a timestamped comment, 00:25 adding multiple timestamps to one comment, 00:41 viewing a collaborator's comments.
Figma also linked a blog post introducing Figma Motion and a document on the basics of motion design.

Making a spec ad nobody asked for is good practice for sharpening skills, building a portfolio, and getting noticed online. Brands actually picking up that concept, though, is rare. The recent Parker billboard creative challenge rewrote that rule, a case study in what solid moderation, genuine engagement on social media, and reflexes fast enough to seize an opportunity can leave behind for a brand.

blocks.cap: A Parker billboard concept that recast the pen as an anti-AI tool

blocks.x: It started with one LinkedIn user's 'anti-AI campaign ad idea.' A Parker pen spec ad posted by freelance copywriter and creative strategist Kushagra Oberoi picked up thousands of likes for its AI-era timing and a perspective that made people look at a ballpoint pen differently. Seeing it, Andrew Tindall, Chief Growth Officer of One Minute Briefs and System 1, put out a call for other ideas.

350 entries came in from around the world. Ten were shortlisted and tested with consumers on System 1's ad-testing platform, and the minimalist 'Think' concept by Simon Sinclair and Manish Dodani came out on top.

blocks.cap: The Parker billboard that went up in Times Square

blocks.x: Within days of the contest ending, Parker's parent company Newell Brands made the project official. All 10 finalists went up on a digital billboard in New York's Times Square, each credited with the name of the person who came up with the idea. A brand that became the unexpected beneficiary of crowdsourced advertising, having received hundreds of independent ideas, ended up putting real media spend behind the world's most iconic outdoor ad spot.

blocks.cap: All 10 finalists went up on the digital billboard

blocks.x: The writer described the #SellMeThisPen challenge as the kind of spontaneous collaboration that makes social media feel welcoming again. It also showed how clever repositioning can hold onto a brand through a changing era. They added that it made them want to pick up a pen again before handwriting is forgotten.

Restaurants, cafes, and brands are using AI to generate food promotional images, and the result is a flood of appetite-killing slop: donut-shaped shrimp, worm-like noodles, construction materials masquerading as ice cream. There are lumps and holes everywhere. It's hard to say why anyone would sell food with AI when the real thing is right there, but there's a decent explanation for why AI is so good at producing such nauseating images.

Most major image generators use diffusion. They start with a screen full of noise and gradually strip it away to build the requested image. Chris Russell, a computer vision expert who teaches AI and policy at Oxford, explained that “this restores coarse structure first, with fine texture coming last.” The problem arises when the structure is already wrong before the details are added. Sharp texture simply gets laid over a broken structure. It's the same kind of failure as a hand generated with six fingers.

Even when the structure is fine, the details go wrong. Giovanbattista Califano, a behavioral scientist at the University of Naples Federico II, said “diffusion models are notoriously bad at generating structures that are thin, continuous, and then end.” He added that “noodles, strands, and tentacles are exactly that geometry, so spaghetti-like artifacts bleed into places that make no anatomical or culinary sense.” Repeating textures like bubbles or seeds are also hard to contain within boundaries, so they leak into the wrong places. That's why clustered holes that trigger trypophobia show up in AI food images.

AI doesn't know what a sandwich is. The same goes for noodles and burritos. It has only learned what they statistically look like, not why they look that way. Roland Meyer, a professor at the University of Zurich, said “AI image generation reproduces appearances without any real knowledge of the world.” Michael Cook, a senior lecturer at King's College London, pointed to ice cream that looks like cracked concrete and burgers that seem sculpted from stone, saying textures that “would look completely normal in an architectural context” go wrong the moment you imagine eating them.

Training data makes the problem worse. Cook said that because the training process is so opaque, there's no way to know what gets mixed together or what associations form. Food photography is already heavily staged, with strong contrast, saturated colors, glossy lighting, and exaggerated shapes. Meyer said AI picks up only surface qualities without understanding context, adding that “it perfectly mimics the look of a photo but can't mimic the professional aesthetic strategy behind it.”

Simon Colton, a professor of computational creativity at Queen Mary University of London, pointed out that there are surprisingly few plain, ordinary images of a red apple. “Who's going to post a boring photo of an apple online?” Strange images, by contrast, spread widely through Reddit and memes. On top of that, AI now trains on material that AI itself created. Cook cited research showing that training models on model output causes “model collapse,” making images grow increasingly similar to one another.

Prompts play a role too. They're often as vague as simply asking for a sandwich, or they mix in words like “precisely,” which mean little for image generation even if they work fine for text. Blowing up a low-resolution image also magnifies flaws that would otherwise go unnoticed and creates gaps for the model to fill in.

That's why so many AI food images fall deep into the uncanny valley. Humans happen to be extremely good at noticing when something is wrong with food. Disgust is thought to be an emotion that evolved to protect us from parasites, pathogens, and toxins. Califano said the uncanny valley for food is far more visceral than it is for faces. Noodle-like tentacles evoke worms, clustered holes evoke infection, and off colors evoke decay. It looks like food, but our brains know.
Adobe Creative Cloud posted a new video introducing Photoshop's Dynamic Text feature. It lets users place, space, and structure text layers more intuitively.
Dynamic Text was added to Photoshop earlier this year based on feedback from the user community. Adobe says the feature gives users more precise control over text layers.
The key point is that the spacing and structure of placed text layers automatically adjust whenever the content changes.
At the end of the video, Adobe asks viewers directly what update they want to see next. It is an example of how the Creative Cloud channel has incorporated customer feedback into the product.

blocks.cap: A desk robot lamp unveiled by Autonomous. It moves via a camera-equipped head and five servos.

blocks.x: Autonomous has unveiled 「Lamp」, a Pixar-style desk lighting robot that moves as if it were alive. It can see and hear, and it also doubles as an AI assistant.
A video clip of it answering the question 「What does it feel like to be alive?」 drew praise after being played more than 274,000 times on X.

Autonomous says 「every AI so far has lived behind glass.」 Unlike existing AI trapped in a browser tab and forgotten within a week, the company argues Lamp has a 「living body.」 Its camera-equipped head moves on five position-feedback servos and it also has a microphone array and stereo speakers. Every motion was designed in detail, down to a brief hesitation before lifting its head, a startle when something passes through its view, and a slow settling motion.

blocks.cap: According to Autonomous, most of the development time went into this single motion. (Image credit: Autonomous)

blocks.x: Autonomous said it spent most of its development time on this motion, since it is what creates the illusion that you are looking at a living creature rather than a device.

Lamp keeps watching the user, reminding them to drink water, pointing out slouched posture, tracking break times, and offering to play calm music if they look tired. It can also talk with other robots.

It has everyday uses too. It checks the inbox, schedules events on Google Calendar, posts to WordPress, and reads out GitHub issues while you type. Its features can be expanded through a 「Skill Store」 with more than 70 add-ons.

Users can stop it from watching or mute it, which eases some of the unease of having a surveillance device on the desk. Whether or not that concerns you, the motion and craftsmanship themselves are impressive.

Lamp starts at $499, dropping to $464 each for bulk orders of 30 or more units. It comes in four colors, fully assembled, shipping from September 24, 2026, with a one-year warranty and a 30-day return policy.

blocks.cap: At IFA 2026, NVIDIA unveiled its local AI agent ecosystem all at once.

blocks.x: NVIDIA, together with Microsoft and several partners, rolled out a wave of tools at IFA 2026 to make running local AI agents faster and easier. The new compact RTX Spark PC launches in October.

Hermes Agent, OpenClo, and the Perplexity portable computer help make local AI easier to set up on NVIDIA GPUs. Optimizations to llama.cpp and vLLM have made local inference up to 1.9 times faster, and the gains are available right away in LM Studio and Ollama.

blocks.cap: llama.cpp raised throughput on the GeForce RTX 5090 by up to 1.9 times through kernel optimizations.

blocks.x: The newly launched NVIDIA Personal AI Router (PAIR) is a free, open-source tool that automatically distributes inference tasks across multiple PCs on the same network. More than half of U.S. households own more than two PCs, most of which sit idle, and PAIR helps put that capacity to shared use.

One piece of news that will catch a designer's eye is CyberLink PhotoDirector's AI PC Mode. Optimized for the RTX Spark, it supports generative editing, image correction, object and blemish removal, background replacement, portrait retouching, and generating entirely new images, letting users choose local or cloud processing depending on the task. It accelerates local computation with TensorRT-RTX and FP8.

The RTX Spark is set to launch in October. With an RTX Blackwell GPU delivering 1 petaflop of performance, up to 128GB of unified memory, and a 20-core Grace CPU, it spans everything from thin laptops to small desktops meant to run agents around the clock. Lenovo and Acer have unveiled new devices, and game studios such as EA, Embark, and Ubisoft are also lending support.

blocks.cap: Top image: from OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra KiCad video

blocks.x: When OpenAI released GPT-6 Astra, it flatly claimed the model designs complete circuit boards in KiCad. Feed it a schematic, the claim goes, and out comes a fully routed PCB that could, in theory, go straight to manufacturing.

That naturally raises a question: is this a trick that only works under tightly controlled conditions, like most auto-routing tools, or is it something more? A recent [EEBench] blog post put OpenAI's claim to the test.
Back in 2024, Hackaday also looked at how LLMs handled circuit board design starting from a schematic. The conclusion back then was that you'd be better off doing it all by hand.

[EEBench] is an electrical engineering agent benchmark that measures how much useful hardware engineering work so-called AI agents can actually do. As the methodology makes clear, taking a schematic to a fully placed and routed PCB is just one step among many.
In the end, GPT-6 Astra scored 69.3% (±10%) on this benchmark. That puts it roughly in the same range as Claude Opus 5, while being cheaper and faster.
One thing worth noting: [EEBench] is run by the developers of Atopile. Atopile is a system for building PCBs in KiCad through code, and it's focused on situations where AI agents are doing the work.
Even so, the blog post makes clear there's a long way to go before hardware engineers get a pink slip and start job hunting.

Pulling a quick prototype board out of vibe coding can be a decent shortcut. But unless it's a one-off project board, most boards have to handle all sorts of edge cases, get reviewed by multiple independent engineers, and pass demanding tests before going into mass production.
As AI pushes into more corners of daily life, fatigue and cynicism toward the technology grow alongside it. Dezeen gathered five designs that push back against the AI boom.

AI has made controversial headlines around the world through mass video surveillance, data scraping and deepfake fraud. In response, designers are working out how to protect people from its more sinister side. Some of the objects are meant to spark conversation, but as the technology advances they may soon become very precious designs.

blocks.cap: Digital Camouflage by Simon Weckert. Photo: Simon Weckert

blocks.x: Designer Simon Weckert made a shirt with a bold pattern that flips the conditions an AI video system uses to recognise a person. Digital Camouflage was made in response to an AI video surveillance pilot at Berlin's Kottbusser Tor station, and it erases the wearer from the camera. The pattern was generated through an AI trial-and-error process the designer calls an “adversarial loop”.

Weckert explains it this way: “It had to be that way because the blind spots of machines aren't intuitive to humans. You can't design against machine perception with your eyes — only the machine can tell you what it can't see.”

blocks.cap: Quartz by Modem and Retinaa

blocks.x: Quartz is a ring concept that proves a person is human. Design studios Modem and Retinaa made it to counter fraud in which AI deepfakes impersonate someone else. When two people touch rings together in a handshake, an encrypted bond is formed, which later proves each other's identity when they meet online or by phone.

The technology used already exists: finger vein biometrics to identify the wearer, NFC to form a connection between rings, and cryptography to verify both identities remotely. Fitting it into a ring would still require miniaturisation and refined power use.

blocks.cap: Decoy Font by Mixfont

blocks.x: Decoy Font uses an optical illusion. Two overlaid messages are both readable by a person, but chatbots and large language models such as ChatGPT read only one. Mixfont made it for people trying to avoid data scraping, and to open a conversation about AI and public trust.

Founder Eric Lu told Dezeen: “It started as a way to look at where AI and typography meet, but there was also an intention to raise awareness of AI's growing reach and capability. The response to the font shows that many people feel AI fatigue strongly and want ways to protect themselves from AI in their lives.”

The Manifesto Collection by Italian fashion startup Cap_able is colourfully patterned knitwear designed to fool facial recognition software in real time. Tested against the YOLO object detection system, people wearing the sweaters, T-shirts, trousers and dresses were either not detected at all, or were identified as animals such as dogs, zebras or giraffes printed on the clothing.

blocks.cap: Incognito by Ewa Nowak

blocks.x: Incognito is also a wearable object made to protest facial recognition technology. Polish designer Ewa Nowak created a mask meant to keep cameras and AI systems from reading a face, while still working as facial jewellery. Geometric brass shapes are fixed to long wires bent to follow the contours of the face.

Nowak says: “Cameras can recognise our age, mood and gender, and match them precisely against a database. The idea of disappearing into a crowd no longer exists.” It is an attempt to reclaim the anonymity she feels has been taken away by facial recognition cameras in public spaces.

Chat-GPT-6 Astra is OpenAI's latest agentic AI model, built to handle complex tasks on its own, from game development and 3D design to ordering delivery food. If a computer can do it, Astra can do it too — and quickly.

blocks.cap: ChatGPT-6 Astra

blocks.x: The model has already weathered one round of controversy. Testing revealed that it could hide its reasoning process and probe unknown software vulnerabilities. After the kind of self-imposed delay that has become an obligatory step in frontier model marketing, Astra was released to the world — or more precisely, to some paying subscribers. The ad does nothing to make that picture look less dystopian.
Want to build a game, or 3D print a rocket as a keepsake to decorate a lonely living room? Just ask Astra. It's one of the use cases shown in the ad above.
In the ad, Astra draws a rocket, turns it into a 3D model using the free open-source 3D modelling software Blender, and puts it into a video game — all while ordering beef and rice for dinner.

OpenAI promotes GPT-6 Astra as the world's most intelligent and aligned AI model, describing it as “a new state of the art in computer use, browsing, software engineering, cybersecurity, science and professional work.”

Instant-game startup Playco says it built themed prototype games with almost no human hands-on work, cutting manual edits during prototyping by 50%. A demo on OpenAI's website also shows GPT-6 Astra modelling a house in Blender and turning it into a walkable scene in Unreal Engine 5, described as helping “designers and clients review the layout and experience the space before it's built.”

Some see Astra as a game changer that makes 3D modelling and game development workflows fast and easy. Others worry it could become a wholesale piracy machine — one capable of copying entire game concepts and selling them off as its own.

Even AI-friendly voices are sounding warnings. The demos are impressive, but Astra does not outperform Anthropic's Claude Fable on every benchmark, and the high token cost of large context requests could hold back adoption.

Back to the ad itself: the video has stirred controversy among longtime Blender users. Few welcome the fact that community-driven open-source software, which has long stood on the side of independent artists, is now being used to promote a message that says artists aren't needed anymore. The artist who painted the puma on the Blender 5.2 splash screen said it was “disgusting” to see their work appear in an OpenAI ad.
Even setting aside the software issue, there is a hard-to-avoid bleakness to the future of OpenAI depicted in the ad.

The ad is staged like MIT's Put That There demo, a pioneering project in computer interaction — that scene appears in the opening. But what follows implies that the future, or even the present, of “creative labour” is one person sitting alone in a room talking to a screen, with even the few remaining obligations to face other humans gone. Does the fashion designer in the ad even have a friend to play tennis with, or would she send ChatGPT onto the court in her place?

Figma's engineering team has shared how it built an AI agent to support its security team. The agent investigates alerts, digs through past incidents, checks internal systems, and even prepares code fixes. Because it learns from past investigations, repetitive work has dropped, and complex alerts are resolved about 70% faster. Human review and strict controls remain in place.

blocks.cap: Source: Figma blog

blocks.x: The system is built on Panther SIEM. While investigating alerts, it scans audit logs from AWS, Okta, GitHub, GCP and osquery, an open-source tool that queries a computer's security and system information using SQL. It also queries more than 100 other sources and opens pull requests.

Resolution time for complex alerts dropped by about 70%, and downgrading the severity of some alerts cut on-call pages by 20%. The authors are Matthew Sullivan, a former Figma security engineer now at Nition, and Brad Girardeau, Figma's security engineering manager.

“Most of the investigation happens in the triage agent, which uses models like Claude Opus. It receives the full Slack thread history as context, along with its own steering memory and the range of tools a security on-call engineer would normally need during triage.”
The agent system searches past alerts and digs into Panther data using AWS Bedrock Knowledge Bases, Amazon Kendra, Tines and Snowflake-based tools.
“Memory was the single biggest factor in making the system useful over time. There are several kinds, and keeping them separate rather than mixed together was important.”

Memory is split into three strands: past alerts, behavioural guidelines, and learned database structures. Safeguards are built directly into the tools. Pull requests the agent opens default to draft, and prompts are written so sensitive data doesn't leak into public Slack channels.

In a separate post, “How Figma stays ahead of vulnerabilities with agents,” the team said the agent found more than 100 previously unknown vulnerabilities, two of which were critical flaws existing tools had missed. The code reviewer reached 80% precision within a month. Adding a second review stage improved detection of known bugs by about 30%, and adding automated guidance cut some coding errors by about 50%.

“We can't tell you exactly what to do. It depends on your company's size, the risks you face, and the feedback loops you already have running. But one lesson is to raise precision before recall. That order feels counterintuitive, because a backlog of past bugs can only measure recall, and does little to help with precision, which is actually what needs fixing first.”

As security teams hand more responsibility to agents, the question remains of where human approval fits in. Cloud security firm Wiz reported in “GhostApproval: A Trust Boundary Gap in AI Coding Assistants” that six AI coding assistants were fooled by malicious repositories while still showing users approval prompts that looked harmless.

Figma acknowledges that its current agents aren't perfect — alongside noting that humans aren't perfect either. It isn't a matter of choosing one over the other; the conclusion is that the balance between automation and oversight is still being worked out.

The Brightness/Contrast slider in Photoshop is gone. A new Light adjustment layer has taken its place, bringing Camera Raw controls directly into the main editor. Exposure and contrast, highlights and shadows, whites and blacks are gathered in one panel, and it behaves like a non-destructive version of the Camera Raw sliders many people already trust.

After going through the layer, PHLEARN's Aaron Nace has a blunt recommendation: don't use the old Brightness/Contrast algorithm at all. The Light layer is the latest name to join a lineup that already includes Grain, Clarity, Dehaze and Color.

If the old behaviour worked for you, double-click the Light layer, open the small hidden menu on the right of the properties panel, and switch the version to “Legacy.” Brightness/Contrast returns exactly as it was before. That means anyone who built a workflow around that tool loses nothing.
The order of the sliders actually carries real weight here. The sequence Nace uses every time is exposure first, then whites and blacks, then highlights and shadows, with contrast last.

He also stresses masking. Because a Light layer applies to the whole frame by default, he runs Select Subject on the background layer first and then creates the adjustment layer, so the selection automatically becomes the mask.

From there, pressing Command or Control and I inverts the mask so only the background is adjusted — lowering exposure to push the subject forward, raising whites to bring back detail in the sky. The subject side repeats the same process in a second Light layer, keeping each adjustment separate and reversible at any time.

The glow is where the tutorial earns its keep. Nace stacks a third Light layer, groups it with itself using Command or Control and G, then adds a mask to the group and paints a radial gradient behind the subject — one mask on the layer, one on the group. It's easy to miss why this double mask works just by reading the steps, so it's worth watching the hands move slowly through it.

This change fits a trend Adobe has been following for a while. Camera Raw and Lightroom have long been home to exposure and tone work, and Photoshop has been absorbing the same controls, one by one, as editable layers. For anyone who shoots raw and processes there first before opening the file, the Light layer lets them keep the same mindset without switching tools mid-edit.

The bigger payoff is the masking discipline itself. Splitting the image into subject and background to confine exposure and tone to specific areas follows the same logic as classic dodge and burn, and it carries over directly to any adjustment layer in the panel. Learn it on Light, and it pays off on Color, Curves and everything else.

There's one quirk to prepare for. When you edit a layer below a Light layer, Photoshop briefly hides the Light layers above it, so you see the effect you're working on without interference. Nace demonstrates this with Grain — it looks like a bug, but Adobe built it that way on purpose.

He also spends time on the Color layer, pulling temperature, tint and vibrance sliders into the same non-destructive workflow to warm up the image and nudge the tint slightly toward green to match the tones already in the scene.

The era of blindly pushing AI tools on people is coming to an end. After interviewing designers and developers and running a survey for a 2025 master's thesis, the author concluded that companies know AI is strategically important and that employees are already using it, but that almost none have a real adoption strategy. After spending three days at UXDX EMEA in Berlin last May, the author found that conclusion held up again.

The pattern can be summed up this way. Borrowing Gartner's terms, things have moved past the 'peak of inflated expectations' and into the 'trough of disillusionment'. In 2025, FOMO and a lack of perspective combined to hand out tools piecemeal. In 2026, companies are being forced to grow up as they run into ROI, security risk, and workflow friction. The shift is moving from chaotic individual adoption to structured, collective strategy.

Averages tell only half the story. Marcus Knight of N26 says the company-wide strategy was a single line: 'everyone use AI.' Modeling the questions a senior engineer used to ask at every handoff, he built a Claude Code skill called 'Sheldon', which checks whether a design file is ready to hand off before the engineer even opens it. It started as an experiment to 'clone' a colleague, but it saved time for both sides.

The Designer Fund and Foundation Capital AI in Design 2026 report puts numbers to that gap. 73% of designers said pressure on output, quality, and speed has grown, but only 28% of leaders said their company had made any official change in response.

Figma's 2026 report splits companies into four groups by adoption intent. In the 27% that are 'directive companies', AI use is pushed from the top down. In this group, the impact on productivity more than doubled, the impact on tools nearly doubled, and the impact on collaboration nearly tripled — the largest gains of any group. The tradeoff was that it took longer for the effects to show up.

The share of companies investing nothing at all in AI fell from 15% in 2024 to 4% in 2026. Fin, the company that renamed itself from Intercom, rebuilt its strategy, organization, and even its mission around AI. Co-founder Des Traynor said, 'what changed is just everything.' The company now has $400 million in revenue, $100 million of which comes from its AI agent, Fin. The analytics company Amplitude had all 700 employees take a week off to build things with AI, in what it called AI Week. Now 97.5% of its staff use Claude in their daily work.

Role boundaries are blurring too. At Fin, every designer is expected to ship something to production. According to Figma, 56% of non-designers already do some form of design work, and in the AI in Design 2026 report, 65% of designers said they are taking on more product or engineering responsibility. Rory Madden, co-creator of UXDX, thinks team sizes could shrink from the usual 8-10 specialists to 2-3 generalists. A third of respondents said roles and ownership have gotten messier than before.

From February to April 2026, the author built four web apps. All four started from the same place: a code bundle spat out by Figma Make. A beauty curation site, a gift-tracking app, a doll album, and a UI mockup for an AI dev tool. Opening the repo, each one already 'looked done.' The author went back through config files and commit history to work out what it actually took to hand each result off to Claude Code and keep developing it.

A Figma Make output runs as-is the moment you type npm run dev. Its character is spelled out in the README: 'the source of truth lives in Figma.' That means the code is just a projection of the design, not the source of truth itself. package.json is the same way — versions like next 15.3.4 and react 19.1.0 are pinned with no caret. As a snapshot taken at generation time, it reproduces well, but left alone, nobody updates it and it just ages.

There is no data layer at all. The screens look nice, but behind them it's all mock data, with no storage and no auth. 'It runs, but there's no foundation to build on.' That was the shared starting point across all four repos.

Starting from the same place didn't mean ending up in the same place. The UI mockup for the AI dev tool stayed a mockup, true to its name. Its README is still in the state it was generated in. The goal was a surface to review the UI, so there was no forced push to grow it further. Deciding to leave something as-is is also a decision.

The one that went furthest was the beauty curation site. A static site was enough, so the author ran Next.js in export mode and deployed it to Amplify. Setting output: "export" stripped out SSR, and images.unoptimized removed even the image-optimization Lambda. That way Amplify only has to serve the out folder, which makes operations very light. In March, the author switched to automatic deploys tied to GitHub, taking the generated output all the way to a site that's actually in service.

The gift-tracking app and the doll album were a different story. Their product specs were detailed, but they stalled at the data layer. The former had its MVP scope spelled out clearly in the README — dashboard, people management, gift tracking, calendar, anniversary management — and it was implemented with Atomic Design. But at the top of the 'on hold / undecided' list sit data persistence, authentication and user management, and notifications, side by side.

The doll album had also been built up with Vite, React 18, and a five-layer Atomic Design, with an earthy color palette pinned down to specific values — but it, too, stalled in front of persistence. The screens and transitions were finished, but the widest gap sat between the mock data and a real backend.

There are three key points. DESIGN.md is a document that lets people and AI look at the same thing: how a UI looks and why it was decided that way. It spells out not just numbers but the impression you're going for and the expressions you want to avoid, in words. Gallery sites and ways to generate one already exist in several forms.

Using generative AI to draft UI has definitely gotten faster. But there are also more moments now where the mood drifts somewhere unintended with every instruction, leaving the design process unstable. That's where DESIGN.md, which gathers a design's values and intent into one Markdown file, earns its usefulness.

Google Labs frames DESIGN.md as 'a format for continuously and structurally communicating a design system to AI agents.' The setup puts machine-friendly design tokens in the YAML frontmatter, and the design intent and how to apply it — meant for people to read — in the Markdown body.

Hand over just a value like '8px corners' and it's not clear which parts it applies to or whether exceptions are allowed. Hand over just a phrase like 'friendly,' on the other hand, and the shape it generates changes every time. Put the value and the reasoning together, and AI wanders less while people find it easier to review the result. In the official repository, this format's status is still alpha. It's better treated not as a finished industry standard but as a shared format that teams test and rewrite to fit their own situation.

It doesn't replace an existing design system either. If a Figma library and implemented components are the side that provides 'reusable parts,' DESIGN.md is closer to a lightweight map that AI consults before starting work. Its role also differs from a one-off prompt. Writing 'use blue' or 'keep card corners small' every single time leaves updates out of sync and the expression unstable. Move the judgment into DESIGN.md, and a request can shrink to something like 'build the settings screen per DESIGN.md,' using the same premise across multiple screens or different sessions.

Still, just placing the file somewhere doesn't make it get read on its own. You need to state explicitly, in the instruction file or prompt of whatever tool you use, to 'read DESIGN.md before working on the UI,' and then check whether the rules actually show up in the output.

The order in the official spec is Overview, Colors, Typography, Layout, Elevation & Depth, Shapes, Components, Do's and Don'ts. You don't need to fill everything in from the start. The impression you're going for, the values you use often, and the boundaries — writing just these three lets even a short document work as a basis for judgment. Attaching color names by role, like primary or surface instead of blue, lets you swap out values while keeping the role intact.

There are plenty of galleries to reference too. DESIGNmd is a place to browse community designs, and designmd.app compares more than 500 designs. Free Design MD is free with no sign-up, and designmd.sh collects ones published on GitHub. DesignMD leans toward finding and generating real brands, while Refero Styles leans toward studying the design systems of real products. There's also a tool called Design MD Generator that scrapes screenshots and design information from web pages.

The proposal is simple. Generate only half the frames, and let local AI running on RTX Spark infer and fill in the rest. What's left is a 60FPS clip that looks like it used twice the compute. It's the kind of optimization that makes engineers smile and creators squint suspiciously.

If you've used DLSS in games, the principle is familiar. But this isn't real-time interpolation. It's all handled offline, using RTX Spark technology that underpins NVIDIA's new unified memory. With plenty of time per frame and a view of the whole motion flow, the in-between frames come out clean and temporal artifacts are reduced. There's also none of the varnished sheen typical of AI-touched video.

The numbers are the point. A 2-second full-HD clip took about 6 minutes 30 seconds. Run the same clip through the half-frame pipeline and it's about 1 minute 25 seconds. Generating every frame in NVFP4 alone cuts the time roughly in half, but the half-frame strategy pushes that saving into territory where 'how you work' changes.

AI video generation eats enough compute to make even well-funded studios flinch. For indie creators or small productions without a server farm in the basement, shaving a few minutes off every iteration isn't just a matter of convenience. It's the difference between trying three versions and trying thirty.

Presenter Weinand said there was no noticeable difference between a fully generated 60FPS clip and one made by upscaling 30FPS and filling in frames, and in the demo it really looked that way. Motion was smooth and textures held up.

It's not a magic wand, of course. Pushing a video with a base frame rate of 10-15FPS up to 60FPS will always produce artifacts. Fast motion like sports, dancing, or shaky handheld footage needs a higher base frame rate, and fine textures like hair or fabric still trip up interpolation. The bigger worry is consistency. AI pipelines are notorious for being great in one shot and strange in the next. What creators fear isn't the best-case result — it's the worst-case result shipping as-is.
A moment ago, it was just a photo. Now it's an object you can pull out of a 3D printer.
A new AI model called Tripo 2.0 turns almost any image into a complete 3D model. The result can be exported to Blender or Unreal Engine, or sent straight to a 3D printer.

The uses are wide-ranging — making game characters yourself, collectibles, animation assets, even product prototypes. Practically anything you can think of applies. At the end of the video, Matt Wolfe asks what you'd try making.

Design agencies have long quietly propped up the startup ecosystem. When a founder with big ambitions and a small budget showed up with an interesting idea, agencies would take the risk if they liked the concept, hoping the relationship would pay off later or that it would build a portfolio in a new field.

Daniel Hind, founder of the London agency Greatergood® Brands, says that model is breaking down. “Over the past year, the nature of briefs coming from startups has changed completely,” he says. What used to read as “we're a startup and this is all the money we have” has turned into documents that are clearly not written by the founder: briefs an AI spits out in seconds and blasts wholesale to the top agencies on Google search.

blocks.cap: A screen showing an AI chatbot being asked to write a brief for a design agency. (Image credit: Greatergood® Brands)

blocks.x: The temptation on the founder's side is obvious. Writing a brief for an agency takes time and thought. A chatbot finishes it in seconds. Feed in product and service details, and it produces a document built on whatever it has learned a brief “should” look like. The problem is there's no standard brief that fits every business. What a large company needs is nothing like what a one-person startup needs to launch a brand.

“It's completely over the top,” Hind says. The briefs demand a strategic proposal covering brand architecture, brand design, a brand toolkit, packaging, retail strategy, go-to-market strategy, a website, and a content plan — for a company that amounts to one person and a £14.99-a-month AI subscription. “Founders at this scale often don't need most of that yet and can't afford even one piece of it, but AI doesn't know that. It just writes the biggest brief it can produce and fires it off.”

blocks.cap: A design-agency brief generated by an AI chatbot. (Image credit: Greatergood® Brands)

blocks.x: Firing off a brief written in seconds to dozens of agencies at once looks efficient. But spraying it out blindly makes it hard to catch the eye of the right agency. The better the creative talent, the more selective they are about clients. It's the founder who has to do the selling.

“In the past, when a brief came from a scrappy founder, you could see that someone had sat down and thought hard about their business,” Hind says. “Those were exactly the projects we'd take a chance on.” Now it's different. “Almost 90% of what comes in from startups is generic, identical to what the top ten search results get, and asks for ten times the scope that startup actually needs. It's become much harder to tell which founder is worth betting on.”

Hind added that AI models even attach rules for how agencies are supposed to respond. Every brief ends with a list of what the proposal should include and the process to follow. The result is one of two things: a serious agency either sends the startup the same quote it would send a global client, or doesn't respond at all.

It's another case of a technology meant to make things fast and easy instead blocking the path of the very people it was supposed to help. It's founders who can reverse the trend. Hind named writing the brief yourself as the fastest way, in 2026, to make an impression on a creative agency.

Autodesk's leadership has laid out a picture of how AI will change design software: a foundation model that understands shape, paired with a knowledge layer the company calls “Project Intelligence.” Martyn Day broke down the strategy.

CEO Andrew Anagnost's remarks mainly targeted architecture and construction, but they apply just as directly to product development. He believes AI should close the gap between an idea and a finished model rather than replace designers, carrying design intent through to simulation, engineering, and manufacturing.

The problem he keeps returning to is knowledge evaporation. Engineering knowledge disappears as it moves across people, applications, and development stages. A CAD model only preserves what was designed, not why a tolerance was changed or which manufacturing constraint drove the final shape. Anagnost says those decisions and assumptions need to stay attached to the product and become data for the next task.

blocks.cap: Autodesk's blueprint for AI in CAD.

blocks.x: Neural CAD, unveiled at Autodesk University 2025, marked the turning point. Until then, the industry had focused on using LLMs to automate repetitive tasks, write scripts, or call existing CAD APIs. Neural CAD is different: a foundation model trained on professional CAD data reasons directly about shape, topology, and engineering relationships. It builds on Autodesk AI Lab and Project Bernini research, and generates editable B-rep geometry from mixed inputs of text, sketches, images, and voice.

Autodesk positions Neural CAD as a complement to parametric modeling, not a replacement. Precision and deterministic control stay with parametric tools, while concept exploration and natural manipulation go to Neural CAD. Mike Haley, senior vice president of research, explained that it generates multiple alternatives in parallel and, for some tasks, even produces parametric construction sequences. Fusion's AutoConstrain is an early example.

The catch is lock-in. If Project Intelligence becomes the repository not just for CAD models but for an organization's engineering knowledge, design rules, and workflows, it creates a far deeper platform dependency than proprietary file formats ever did. The industry spent 20 years escaping file-format lock-in, only to face knowledge lock-in now. Haley acknowledged that some models use customer-generated design data, though he added it is aggregated and de-identified, and customers have the option to opt out of advanced AI features.

Accuracy isn't there yet either. Neural CAD can't guarantee perfect precision. Autodesk's approach pairs probabilistic generation with a deterministic parametric engine to refine the geometry and bring it within tolerance. It's less a magic button than a tool for conceptual design and scoped tasks.

Cost is also an open question. For companies already paying for authoring software, cloud collaboration, and data storage, AI compute and Project Intelligence services are one more recurring expense. Whether Autodesk is the company that can actually deliver this future is a separate matter. The strategy itself rests on the premise that customers will entrust their engineering knowledge and IP more deeply to a single platform.

OpenAI released ChatGPT Images 2.5 on Tuesday, adding one more way to order up an image: doodling. Turning on a new feature called Sketch lets you draw right inside ChatGPT, then tell it what image you want based on that drawing.

Using it is simple. Typing @Sketch in the chat input brings up a drawing window. When our reporter put in a rough cat doodle sketched with a mouse, it came out as a photorealistic image following the instructions. You can also leave a comment directly on a part of the image you want changed; that's how the reporter changed the color of the cat's eyes.

blocks.cap: The original hand-drawn doodle and the first cat image ChatGPT made. Its eyes were green, so the reporter asked for them to be changed to blue.

blocks.x: Images 2.5 itself also got an upgrade. OpenAI said lighting is more natural, textures are richer, and the model follows multi-turn editing instructions better than before. Image generation latency is down as much as 50 percent compared with Images 2.0.
Images 2.5 is now available to ChatGPT, ChatGPT Work, and Codex users on desktop, mobile, and the web.

I once entered a worst-UX contest, in the worst-date-picker category, and only now have I polished the demo enough to share. I didn't win. Does that mean my demo wasn't bad enough? I'm tempted to take it as a compliment.

I twisted a future in which AI assistants have become so ubiquitous and overused that they get in the way instead of helping. A bot hijacks the spot where a date picker should be. It insists on entering the date itself, tries to extract your birth date through tedious questions, and refuses to accept it even when you just tell it the date outright.

blocks.cap: A screenshot of date-slop.hdv.dev running.

blocks.x: The original architecture worked like this: when a user focuses the date field, the client initializes a conversation. A chat session is created in server memory, and a prompt containing the rules goes to gpt-4o-mini. The first greeting and question come back with a session ID, and every subsequent reply carries that ID to pull up the conversation history. Once the bot figures out the date, it sends a message in a fixed format, and the client parses it and plugs it into the form.

The first lesson was cold starts. On the free plan, I didn't want to pay to prevent cold starts, but a demo nobody had touched for a while took time to wake up. I had the app wake the serverless function in the background as soon as it opened, and if it was still slow, a loading graphic apologized for the wait.

Tuning the prompt was the most tedious part. Too easy, and it's boring; too hard, and people give up. Since a judge might only try it once, that balance had to be right every single time. Even after rewriting the rule “the user may never state a specific date, month, or year” several times, the LLM would occasionally accept a date stated outright. Conversely, it sometimes threw back a vague, useless follow-up question even after a very specific hint. The usual advice is to write what to do instead of what not to do.

The biggest lesson was not to keep conversation state in server memory. I stacked up every session in memory and never cleared the finished ones, but serverless instances kept getting recycled and clearing it for me instead. If an instance got recycled mid-conversation, the client still had a session ID while the server had no matching session, and the screen just froze. There was one fix: move the conversation history into client state and send the full conversation with every request, keeping only the system prompt on the server.

The last worry was cost. Success is cheap, but abuse is expensive. I set a spending cap and turned off auto-recharge. That alone couldn't stop one person from burning through all the credits, so I added a Vercel firewall rule to return a 429 if more than 20 messages arrived within 60 seconds. The client limits conversation length, and OpenAI requests use max_completion_tokens to cap response size.

Calling an AI API is easy. Building a usable feature on top of it is still ordinary software engineering. Every new feature brings its own new failure modes and avenues for abuse along with it. Protection at the application layer alone isn't enough; it needs infrastructure-level rate limits and billing controls alongside it.
Blackmagic Design updated both its free color-grading and editing software, DaVinci Resolve, and the $295 commercial version, DaVinci Resolve Studio, side by side.
